rows.content:
# Vertical Openings and Floor Roof Construction

---

## Learning Goal

After reading this article, you should be able to:

Apply fire protection requirements for vertical openings (stairs, shafts, chutes, ducts) under PD 1096 Rule XII and for floor/roof construction under Rule VIII; determine when draft stops, fire dampers, and firestopping are required; calculate maximum permitted floor opening sizes unprotected vs protected; identify the shaft enclosure fire-rating required by building height.

## Module Header

| Field | Details |
|---|---|
| **Module Focus** | Escalator/Elevator Enclosure Requirements, Fire-Rated Shaft Design, Floor Lateral Bracing & Roof Wind Loads |
| **Legal Basis (PH)** | PD 1096, Rule XII, Sections 1204–1206; RA 9514 (Fire Code of the Philippines) |
| **IBC Counterpart** | IBC Section 713 (Shaft Enclosures), Table 601 (Fire-Resistance Requirements by Construction Type) |
| **LEA Area** | Area 2 — Structural Design, Utilities & Materials (30% of exam weight) |
| **Difficulty** | Intermediate |
| **Spaced Repetition** | Review on Day 1, Day 3, Day 7, and Day 14 |

---

## Hook Scenario

Picture yourself reviewing the working drawings for a new 10-storey mixed-use development in Ortigas Center. The building has two passenger elevators, one service elevator, and — critically — two escalators connecting the ground floor retail arcade to the second-floor cinema lobby. During the building permit review, the Building Official's fire safety evaluator flags three issues: the escalator opening design has no draft curtain shown on the reflected ceiling plan, the floor-to-floor opening for a feature staircase in the atrium exceeds 25% of the wall length at the 3-hour separation zone, and the roof framing schedule lists a wind load of only 80 kg/sq.m — below the minimum required by Sec. 1206.

Each of these findings can trigger a permit denial or, worse, a fire-safety citation after occupancy. Sections 1204–1206 of PD 1096 are the referee for every vertical opening, every shaft wall, every beam-to-girder connection, and the minimum wind resistance of every roof in the Philippines. Pass this module, and you will know exactly what the evaluator is looking for before the plans leave your table.

---

## Core Concepts

### Concept 1: Escalator Openings — Draft Curtains and Sprinkler Geometry (Sec. 1204)

Escalators present a unique fire hazard because the moving steps create a continuous open path between floor levels — a chimney effect that can carry fire, smoke, and toxic gases from one storey to the next within seconds. PD 1096 Sec. 1204 addresses this with two simultaneous countermeasures:

**Draft Curtain Requirement:**
- A draft curtain must extend **at least 200 mm** downward from the ceiling on **all sides** of the escalator opening.
- Purpose: the curtain confines smoke and heat at the ceiling level, preventing horizontal spread before the sprinklers activate.
- Material: must be of incombustible construction; glass, metal, or approved non-combustible board.

**Sprinkler Ring Requirement:**
- Automatic sprinklers must be installed around the **perimeter** of each escalator opening.
- The sprinklers must be positioned **within 600 mm** of the draft curtain (measured horizontally from the curtain face).
- Maximum sprinkler spacing along the perimeter: **1.80 m center to center**.
- Purpose: the water curtain from the sprinklers (combined with the draft curtain) creates a drenching barrier at the opening, suppressing fire spread between floors without requiring a full shaft enclosure.

Together, the draft curtain + sprinkler ring system is the Philippine code's alternative to full shaft enclosure for escalators — it provides compartmentalization through active (sprinklers) and passive (curtain) means simultaneously.

### Concept 2: The Three-Hour Separation Opening Limits (Sec. 1204)

When a building's occupancy separation requires a **3-hour fire-resistive rating** between areas (e.g., high-hazard vs. ordinary occupancy), any opening in those separation walls is strictly controlled:

1. **Maximum aggregate opening**: All openings in any wall requiring 3-hour separation must not exceed **25% of the total wall length**.
2. **Maximum single opening**: No individual opening in that wall may exceed **10.00 sq.m**.
3. **Vertical enclosure**: Floor-level openings (holes, shafts, atria) within a 3-hour separation zone must be protected by vertical enclosures constructed to a minimum of **2-hour fire-resistive** construction.
4. **Opening assemblies in enclosure**: The openings within those 2-hour enclosure walls must be protected by **3-hour fire assemblies** (i.e., fire doors or shutters with a 3-hour rating).

This creates a layered system: the shaft wall itself is 2-hour rated, but the door or damper in that wall must be rated for 3 hours — matching the occupancy separation requirement even though the wall rating is lower.

### Concept 3: Floor Construction — Lateral Bracing of Beams (Sec. 1205)

Sec. 1205 contains a frequently overlooked but exam-testable requirement: floor construction must provide a **means to prevent lateral buckling of beams and girders**. Lateral-torsional buckling is the failure mode of long unbraced flexural members — when a beam is loaded vertically, its compression flange can buckle sideways before reaching full flexural capacity.

The code mandates that floor systems — whether reinforced concrete slabs, composite steel-deck systems, or timber framing — inherently brace the beams they rest upon. In practice:
- A concrete slab cast monolithically with or composite-connected to steel beams provides continuous lateral restraint to the top (compression) flange.
- Timber floor systems require blocking between joists or lateral bridging.
- Long-span steel transfer beams that do not have a slab bearing directly on them must have discrete lateral braces at prescribed intervals per the NSCP.

The exam will not ask for specific bracing intervals (those are in NSCP/AISC), but will ask whether floor construction has a duty to prevent lateral buckling — the answer is yes, per Sec. 1205.

### Concept 4: Roof Wind Load — The 120 kg/sq.m Minimum (Sec. 1206)

Per Sec. 1206, roof construction and covering must resist a **minimum wind load of 120 kg/sq.m** applied to the **vertical projection** of the roof. This is not a wind pressure on the inclined roof surface — it is the force calculated against the vertical silhouette of the roof as seen from the windward direction.

This 120 kg/sq.m figure is the **floor**, not a design value — actual wind loads in typhoon-prone regions of the Philippines (Visayas, Eastern Luzon, Bicol) will be substantially higher per NSCP wind maps. The code baseline ensures that no roof in the Philippines is designed to resist less than this minimum, regardless of location.

Roof covering must match the fire-resistance type of construction required for the building. Type I construction (highest fire resistance) requires non-combustible roof coverings; Type V (lowest) permits combustible materials subject to the fire district classification.

### Concept 5: Elevator Enclosures (Sec. 1204)

Elevator shafts (hoistways) must be enclosed per Sec. 1204. The enclosure serves dual functions: containing fire and smoke within the shaft (preventing chimney-effect spread between floors) and protecting passengers from falling objects and mechanical hazards. The fire rating of elevator enclosures in the Philippine system is tied to the **occupancy separation hours** applicable between the served floors — unlike the IBC, which assigns ratings based on the number of stories served.

---

## PH vs. USA Comparative Analysis

The most significant divergence between Philippine and American codes in this topic area is the **method of assigning shaft fire ratings**. The IBC uses a simple, story-count rule that is easy to apply uniformly. The Philippine code ties shaft ratings to the more nuanced occupancy separation requirements — which means the rating depends on what is on each side of the shaft, not just how tall the building is.

| Topic | PH — PD 1096 (Rule XII, Sec. 1204–1206) | USA — IBC (Sec. 713, Table 601) |
|---|---|---|
| **Escalator protection method** | Draft curtain (≥ 200mm) + automatic sprinklers within 600mm, max 1.80m spacing | IBC Sec. 713.14: Escalator openings permitted with sprinkler + draft curtain (similar approach); some editions require full shaft enclosure |
| **Shaft fire rating basis** | Tied to occupancy separation hours for the areas served | IBC Sec. 713.4: 1-hour for shafts ≤ 3 storeys; 2-hour for shafts ≥ 4 storeys |
| **Shaft ≤ 3 storeys** | Rating per occupancy separation (could be 1- or 2-hour depending on occupancy mix) | 1-hour fire-resistive per IBC Sec. 713.4 |
| **Shaft ≥ 4 storeys** | Rating per occupancy separation (could be 2- or 3-hour) | 2-hour fire-resistive per IBC Sec. 713.4 |
| **Max wall opening (3-hr separation)** | 25% of wall length; single opening max 10.00 sq.m | IBC Sec. 707.6: Max 25% aggregate of wall area; single opening max 156 sq.ft (~14.5 sq.m) |
| **Enclosure wall rating** | Min 2-hour for enclosures within 3-hour separation zones | 1- or 2-hour per Sec. 713.4 based on stories |
| **Opening assembly rating** | 3-hour fire assembly at openings in 2-hour enclosure walls | IBC Table 716.1: Opening protectives per wall rating; 1.5-hour for 2-hour walls |
| **Floor lateral bracing** | Required by code language (Sec. 1205) | AISC 360 Appendix 6; IBC defers to referenced structural standards |
| **Minimum roof wind load** | 120 kg/sq.m on vertical projection (Sec. 1206) | ASCE 7 Chapter 26–27: Wind loads by zone; no universal minimum floor |
| **Roof covering requirements** | Per type of construction | IBC Table 1505.1: Roof covering by construction type and fire district |
| **Governing fire code** | RA 9514 (Fire Code) supplements PD 1096 | NFPA 101 (Life Safety Code) and NFPA 13 (Sprinklers) supplement IBC |

**Key Philosophical Difference — Shaft Ratings**: The IBC's story-count rule (1-hour for ≤3 stories, 2-hour for ≥4 stories) is simple and universal, making code compliance straightforward but potentially over-prescribing fire ratings in low-risk situations. The Philippine approach, which ties shaft ratings to occupancy separation requirements, is more nuanced and risk-sensitive — but requires the design architect to first determine the correct occupancy separation for the areas served before selecting the shaft wall rating. This makes the Philippine system harder to apply mechanically but more architecturally responsive.

---

## Hard Data / Cheat Sheet Table

| Parameter | Value | Code Reference |
|---|---|---|
| Escalator draft curtain depth | ≥ 200 mm on all sides of opening | Sec. 1204 |
| Sprinkler proximity to draft curtain | Within 600 mm of curtain | Sec. 1204 |
| Max sprinkler spacing at escalator perimeter | 1.80 m center to center | Sec. 1204 |
| Max aggregate opening in 3-hr separation wall | 25% of wall length | Sec. 1204 |
| Max single opening in 3-hr separation wall | 10.00 sq.m | Sec. 1204 |
| Min rating of vertical enclosure walls | 2-hour fire-resistive | Sec. 1204 |
| Fire assembly rating at enclosure openings | 3-hour | Sec. 1204 |
| Floor construction duty | Prevent lateral buckling of beams/girders | Sec. 1205 |
| Minimum roof wind load (vertical projection) | 120 kg/sq.m | Sec. 1206 |
| IBC shaft rating (≤ 3 storeys) | 1-hour fire-resistive | IBC Sec. 713.4 |
| IBC shaft rating (≥ 4 storeys) | 2-hour fire-resistive | IBC Sec. 713.4 |
| IBC max single opening (fire barrier) | ~14.5 sq.m (156 sq.ft) | IBC Sec. 707.6 |
| IBC max aggregate opening | 25% of wall area | IBC Sec. 707.6 |
| PH escalator sprinkler — activation type | Automatic | Sec. 1204 |
| Elevator shaft — enclosure required | Yes (all elevator openings) | Sec. 1204 |

---

## Cross-Referencing

### RA 9514 (Fire Code of the Philippines, 2019 IRR)
RA 9514 and its Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) are the operational fire-safety overlay to PD 1096's structural provisions. Where Sec. 1204 establishes the passive fire-resistance requirements for shaft enclosures, RA 9514 governs:
- **Sprinkler system design standards** (NFPA 13 as adopted in the Philippines).
- **Fire alarm integration** — shafts require smoke detectors and are connected to the building's fire alarm control panel.
- **Fire dampers** at HVAC penetrations through shaft enclosure walls.
- **Occupancy load and egress** considerations that affect how many and what size openings are permitted.

The design team must satisfy both codes simultaneously: PD 1096 sets the minimum construction requirements for the shaft wall; RA 9514 governs the active systems (sprinklers, alarms, dampers) protecting penetrations through those walls.

### Rule VI — Fire-Resistive Requirements
Rule VI of PD 1096 establishes the fire-resistance hours required for different types of construction and occupancy groups. The shaft rating in Sec. 1204 is not standalone — it must be read in conjunction with the Type of Construction and occupancy group table in Rule VI to determine whether a 1-hour or 2-hour (or higher) enclosure is required for a given building. For example, a mixed Group E (Business) and Group H (Storage) occupancy requiring a 3-hour separation triggers the 10.00 sq.m opening cap and the 2-hour vertical enclosure with 3-hour fire assemblies.

### NSCP — Structural Requirements for Floor Systems
The structural adequacy of floor systems to prevent lateral buckling (Sec. 1205) is detailed in NSCP Chapter 5 (Steel) and Chapter 6 (Concrete). For steel floor systems, NSCP Table 502.2.1 gives maximum unbraced lengths for beams. For concrete, the slab-to-beam interface inherently provides continuous lateral restraint, satisfying the intent of Sec. 1205 when designed per NSCP standards.

### NSCP Chapter 2 — Wind Load Provisions
The 120 kg/sq.m minimum wind load for roofs (Sec. 1206) is the administrative floor established by PD 1096. Actual design wind pressures are calculated per NSCP Chapter 2 (Wind Loads), which uses a wind speed map of the Philippines. Typhoon-prone regions may produce design wind pressures of 200–300 kg/sq.m or higher, well above the 120 kg/sq.m NBCP minimum. The NSCP figure always governs when it exceeds the NBCP baseline.

---

## Active Learning Techniques

### Memory Aid — "200-600-1.8" (The Escalator Trio)
The three escalator sprinkler/curtain numbers form a progression: **200mm curtain depth → 600mm sprinkler distance from curtain → 1.8m between sprinklers**. Visualize a cross-section: the curtain hangs 200mm down, the nearest sprinkler head is 600mm away, and the next sprinkler is 1,800mm from the first.

Say it as: *"Two hundred — six hundred — eighteen hundred."* Each number is three times the last ÷ something — but more reliably, just chain them: **2-6-18** (in units of 100mm).

### Memory Aid — "25-10-2-3" (The Three-Hour Separation Rule)
For a 3-hour separation:
- **25%** of wall length — maximum aggregate openings
- **10 sq.m** — maximum single opening
- **2-hour** — minimum enclosure wall rating
- **3-hour** — fire assembly required at openings in enclosure

Read it as: *"Twenty-five percent of the wall, ten square meters max per hole, two-hour walls, three-hour doors."*

### Memory Aid — "120 Kilos Against the Wind"
Roof wind load minimum: **120 kg/sq.m on vertical projection**. Associate "120" with the number of minutes in 2 hours — a memory bridge. Or simply: *"A Philippine roof must withstand at least 120 kilograms per square meter of wind."*

### If/Then Scenarios

**If** the building has escalators connecting 5 floors of a department store…
**Then** each escalator floor opening requires a draft curtain ≥ 200mm on all sides AND automatic sprinklers within 600mm of the curtain at max 1.80m spacing — all of this per Sec. 1204.

**If** a wall between a Group H warehouse and a Group E office area requires a 3-hour occupancy separation…
**Then** total openings in that wall must not exceed 25% of wall length, no single opening may be larger than 10.00 sq.m, and any floor opening must be enclosed in a 2-hour wall fitted with 3-hour fire assemblies.

**If** the structural engineer proposes a long-span steel transfer beam at the ground floor that has no floor slab directly connected to it…
**Then** discrete lateral bracing is required per Sec. 1205 and the NSCP — the floor construction must prevent lateral buckling of that beam.

**If** the structural drawings show a minimum design roof wind load of 100 kg/sq.m…
**Then** this is non-compliant per Sec. 1206 — the minimum is 120 kg/sq.m on the vertical projection, regardless of the project's location or wind zone.

---

## Exam Traps

### Trap 1: Confusing the Enclosure Wall Rating with the Fire Assembly Rating (Sec. 1204)
A classic board exam setup: a question describes a shaft enclosure in a 3-hour occupancy separation zone and asks for the required fire rating of (a) the enclosure wall and (b) the door within that wall.

The trap: candidates assume both are rated the same as the occupancy separation (3 hours). In fact:
- **Enclosure wall**: minimum **2-hour** fire-resistive construction.
- **Fire assembly** (door/shutter at opening): **3-hour** — matching the occupancy separation requirement.

The enclosure wall and the door/assembly that penetrates it carry **different ratings**. This is a deliberate code design: the opening assembly compensates for the lower wall rating by being rated for the full occupancy separation requirement.

### Trap 2: Sprinkler Distance — From the Curtain, Not the Opening Edge
The 600 mm measurement for sprinkler placement at escalator openings is measured **from the draft curtain** — not from the edge of the floor opening. The draft curtain is set in from the opening edge (it hangs from the ceiling slab edge above the escalator), so the 600 mm begins at the curtain face, not at the slab edge. An exam question may describe dimensions from the opening edge and ask whether the sprinkler placement is code-compliant — always re-reference the measurement to the curtain.

### Trap 3: The 120 kg/sq.m Roof Wind Load Is on the Vertical Projection
The 120 kg/sq.m figure in Sec. 1206 applies to the **vertical projection** of the roof — the area of the roof as projected onto a vertical plane perpendicular to the wind direction. This is not the same as the total inclined roof surface area. A steeply sloped gable roof has a large inclined surface but a relatively small vertical projection (the gable end). An exam question may present a flat roof and an inclined roof and ask for the design wind load — both use vertical projection, but the inclined roof's vertical projection is the wall-silhouette area, not the slope area. Do not multiply the inclined area by cos(θ) or sin(θ) — the code simply says "vertical projection."

---

## Active Recall Questions

**Question 1**

An architect is designing the second-floor opening for escalators in a large shopping mall in Cebu City. The escalator opening is 3.60 m × 1.20 m (plan dimensions). Which of the following correctly describes the required passive and active fire protection for this opening per PD 1096, Rule XII, Sec. 1204?

A. A 150 mm draft curtain on two sides (parallel to travel direction) and sprinklers at 2.00 m spacing within 800 mm of the curtain  
B. A 200 mm draft curtain on all sides and automatic sprinklers within 600 mm of the curtain at maximum 1.80 m center-to-center spacing  
C. Full shaft enclosure of 2-hour fire-resistive construction with a 3-hour fire assembly at each escalator landing  
D. A 200 mm draft curtain on all sides only — no sprinklers required if the mall has a central fire alarm system  

> **Answer: B — 200mm draft curtain on all sides and sprinklers within 600mm at max 1.80m c/c**
>
> Per Sec. 1204, escalator openings require: (1) a draft curtain of **at least 200 mm** on **all sides** of the opening (not just two sides), and (2) automatic sprinklers installed within **600 mm** of the draft curtain at **maximum 1.80 m center-to-center** spacing. Option A is wrong on the curtain depth (150mm, not 200mm), the curtain coverage (two sides only, not all sides), and sprinkler proximity (800mm exceeds the 600mm limit). Option C applies the full shaft enclosure requirement — Sec. 1204 offers the draft curtain + sprinkler combination precisely as an alternative to full enclosure. Option D omits the mandatory sprinkler ring — a fire alarm system does not substitute for the required active suppression at the escalator opening.

---

**Question 2**

A firewall is required to achieve a 3-hour fire-resistive occupancy separation between a Group H (storage) warehouse and a Group B (residential) condominium tower that share a common wall. The wall is 20.00 m long. A building manager requests a 12.00 sq.m double door opening and a 4.00 sq.m service window in that wall. Are these openings compliant with PD 1096, Rule XII, Sec. 1204?

A. Yes — the total opening (16.00 sq.m) is less than 25% of the wall area  
B. No — the 12.00 sq.m double door exceeds the maximum single opening of 10.00 sq.m  
C. Yes — as long as 3-hour fire assemblies are installed at both openings  
D. No — no openings are permitted in a 3-hour occupancy separation wall under any circumstances  

> **Answer: B — The 12.00 sq.m double door exceeds the 10.00 sq.m maximum single opening limit**
>
<LawCallout code="pd1096" section="Rule IV - Vertical Openings">


Per Sec. 1204, for a wall requiring 3-hour fire-resistive occupancy separation: (1) aggregate openings must not exceed 25% of wall length (25% × 20.00m = 5.00m — note this is measured by length, not area), and (2) no single opening may exceed 10.00 sq.m. The 12.00 sq.m double door violates the single-opening maximum regardless of the total. The 4.00 sq.m service window alone would be compliant on its own. Option A incorrectly applies the 25% limit to area rather than length and ignores the 10.00 sq.m single-opening cap. Option C is wrong because 3-hour fire assemblies alone cannot cure an oversize opening — the opening itself must first comply. Option D is incorrect — openings are permitted, subject to the 25%-of-length and 10.00 sq.m limits.


</LawCallout>

---

**Question 3**

A structural engineer proposes a minimum design wind load of 95 kg/sq.m on the vertical projection of the roof for a new 3-storey school building in a low-wind-hazard municipality in Mindanao. Is this compliant with PD 1096, Rule XII, Sec. 1206, and if not, what is the minimum required value?

A. Compliant — local wind hazard surveys may reduce the minimum load below 120 kg/sq.m  
B. Non-compliant — the minimum is 150 kg/sq.m for educational occupancies per Sec. 1206  
C. Non-compliant — Sec. 1206 requires a minimum of 120 kg/sq.m on the vertical projection regardless of location  
D. Compliant — Sec. 1206 applies only to buildings taller than 3 storeys  

> **Answer: C — Non-compliant; the minimum is 120 kg/sq.m on the vertical projection**
>
> Per Sec. 1206, roof construction must resist **at least 120 kg/sq.m** applied to the **vertical projection** of the roof. This is an absolute minimum with no exception for low-wind municipalities, low-rise buildings, or occupancy type. The 95 kg/sq.m proposed load is 20.8% below the mandatory floor. Local wind surveys may justify higher loads (especially in typhoon corridors), but they cannot justify values below the Sec. 1206 minimum. Option A is incorrect — local surveys cannot reduce the mandatory minimum. Option B invents an occupancy-specific minimum of 150 kg/sq.m that does not exist in Sec. 1206. Option D is wrong — Sec. 1206 applies to all buildings regardless of height.

---

## Spaced Repetition Reminder

**Session 1 (Today):** Memorize the "200-600-1.8" escalator trio and the "25-10-2-3" separation rule chain. Read the Exam Traps section carefully — the wall vs. assembly rating distinction is a perennial board question.

**Session 2 (Day 3):** Without looking at the article, write out the complete requirements for a 3-hour occupancy separation with floor openings. Then check against the Cheat Sheet.

**Session 3 (Day 7):** Reconstruct the PH vs. USA comparison table from memory, focusing on the shaft rating difference (PH: tied to occupancy separation hours; IBC: story-count rule). Explain it to a study partner.

**Session 4 (Day 14):** Review only the Active Recall Questions. If you answer all three correctly and can explain each wrong answer, this module is mastered.

*These articles are LEA board exam review materials based on PD 1096 (National Building Code of the Philippines) and cross-referenced with IBC provisions for comparative analysis. Always verify against the current edition of the implementing rules and regulations.*

---



---

## Exam Tip

LEA Trap: Vertical openings ≤ 1.0 m² may be UNPROTECTED if they do not connect more than 3 stories. Openings > 1.0 m² require 1-hour enclosure (or 2-hour for buildings > 4 stories). The 1.0 m² threshold and the 3-story limit are both frequently tested.

## Cross‑References

**Fire Resistive Construction Ratings**, **Stairs Handrails Guardrails**, **Vent Shafts And Ventilation**, **Penthouses And Roof Structures**

rows.title: Minimum Requirements Group A Dwellings
rows.content:
# Minimum Requirements Group A Dwellings

**Module Focus:** Rule VII, Sections 708-709 — PD 1096 (National Building Code of the Philippines)
**LEA Area:** Building Technology / Architectural Design & Site Planning
**Difficulty:** Intermediate
**Spaced Repetition:** Return in 3 days to re-answer the Active Recall questions without looking at the answers.

---

## The Real-World Hook

## Learning Goal

After reading this article, you should be able to:

Apply the minimum requirements for Group A (Residential) dwellings under PD 1096 Rule VII: minimum lot area, floor area, setback, light and ventilation, and sanitary facilities per unit type (single-family, duplex, apartment, townhouse); distinguish Group A-1 through A-4 by density and configuration.
---


It is 6:30 in the morning in a barangay in Cavite. The Dela Cruz family — father, mother, grandmother, and three children — wake up in a house that is legally classified as a Group A dwelling, a single-family residence. The kitchen is barely large enough for two people to work in simultaneously. The toilet is tucked under the staircase. The youngest child's bedroom gets no direct light from outside; a borrowed window faces a narrow court between the house and the next property. The house was built without a building permit, without a licensed architect, without any reference to the National Building Code of the Philippines.

Three years later, the family is selling the property to buy something bigger. A buyer's due diligence reveals the house was never issued a Certificate of Occupancy. The municipal Building Official inspects the structure and finds that the toilet room's area is only 0.85 square meters — below the 1.20 square meters required by PD 1096. The habitable rooms fail the minimum 6.00 square meter floor area rule. The corner lot coverage is at 92%, exceeding the 90% maximum. The slea falls through. The family loses two months of paperwork, a lawyer's fees, and the buyer's earnest money.

This scenario repeats itself thousands of times across the Philippines every year. The minimum requirements for Group A dwellings under PD 1096, Rule VII, Sections 708-709 — and the room dimension rules under Rule VIII, Sections 805-806 — are not bureaucratic afterthoughts. They are the difference between a home that can be legally sold, refinanced, insured, and occupied versus one that exists in a grey zone of non-compliance. For the LEA candidate, these numbers are not merely memorizable facts; they are the professional obligations you will carry every time you sign and seal a residential plan.

## Core Concepts

### Principle 1: Lot Occupancy Limits — 90% Corner Lot, 80% Inside Lot

Per PD 1096, Rule VII, Sec. 708(a), **a Group A dwelling shall occupy not more than 90% of a corner lot and not more than 80% of an inside lot.**

These percentages refer to the ratio of the building footprint (ground floor area of the structure, including all projections) to the total lot area. Let's be precise about the definitions:

- **Corner lot:** A lot bounded by two intersecting streets. Because it has frontage on two sides, it typically enjoys greater access, visibility, and light, hence the more generous 90% maximum coverage.
- **Inside lot:** A lot bounded by a street on one side only, with neighboring properties on the remaining sides. More constrained, hence the tighter 80% maximum.
- **Lot coverage (or PSO — Percentage of Site Occupancy):** The ratio of the building footprint to the total lot area, expressed as a percentage.

**Why these limits exist:** Lot coverage limits preserve open space within the lot for air circulation, rainwater drainage, emergency access, and the psychological well-being of occupants. In the Philippines' tropical climate, unbuilt lot area also reduces heat island effect, allows for natural drainage (critical given frequent typhoons), and provides buffer space for the structural setback from property lines.

These maximums interact with the **Civil Code of the Philippines**, which Sec. 708(a) explicitly cross-references: the dwelling shall be at least **2 meters from the property line**, subject to Civil Code easements of light and view. This 2-meter setback from the property line creates a mandatory strip of open space around the structure that cannot be built upon. On a narrow lot, this 2-meter setback can significantly reduce the buildable area, potentially making the 80% (inside lot) or 90% (corner lot) maximums academic — the setback constraint may be more binding.

**Calculating buildable area:** If a client owns a 150 sq m inside lot, the maximum building footprint is 150 × 0.80 = 120 sq m. However, the 2-meter setback from all property lines further constrains this. If the lot is 10 m × 15 m, the setback reduces the buildable area to (10 − 4) × (15 − 4) = 6 × 11 = 66 sq m — far less than 120 sq m. The more restrictive constraint governs.

### Principle 2: Minimum Room Sizes for Habitable Rooms — 6.00 sq m, Least Dimension 2.00 m

Per PD 1096, Rule VIII, Sec. 806(1)(a), **rooms for human habitation (bedrooms, living rooms, dining rooms, multi-purpose rooms) require a minimum floor area of 6.00 sq m with a least dimension of no less than 2.00 m.**

Two numbers, two conditions — both must be satisfied simultaneously:

1. **Minimum area:** 6.00 sq m. A room that is 3 m × 2 m = 6 sq m just barely qualifies. A room that is 2.5 m × 2.5 m = 6.25 sq m qualifies on area but must also pass the least-dimension test.
2. **Least dimension:** 2.00 m. This is the shortest side of the room. A room that is 6 m × 1 m = 6 sq m fails because the least dimension (1 m) is below 2.00 m. A corridor-like room with sufficient area but a narrow width is not a habitable room under the Code.

The least-dimension requirement ensures the room is actually usable as a living space and not a glorified hallway. The Philippine minimum of 6.00 sq m represents an absolute floor — it is the smallest room that the Code considers habitable. Most professional practice targets significantly larger dimensions for livability and marketability.

**Referenced provision:** The Sec. 708(e) minimum standards for Group A dwellings explicitly cross-reference Sec. 806 for room sizes. This connection between Rule VII and Rule VIII is frequently tested on board exams in the form of "which section governs the minimum room size for a Group A dwelling?" — the correct answer cites Rule VIII, Sec. 806, invoked by Rule VII, Sec. 708(e).

### Principle 3: Minimum Kitchen Size — 3.00 sq m, Least Dimension 1.50 m

Per PD 1096, Rule VIII, Sec. 806(1)(b), **kitchens require a minimum floor area of 3.00 sq m with a least dimension of no less than 1.50 m.**

Again, both conditions apply simultaneously. A kitchen that is 2 m × 1.5 m = 3.00 sq m qualifies. A kitchen that is 3 m × 1 m = 3.00 sq m fails (least dimension = 1.0 m, below 1.50 m). The 1.50 m minimum width is critical: it ensures a person can stand at the counter and another can pass behind them, which is the ergonomic minimum for a functional kitchen.

**Philippine context:** In informal settlements and socialized housing, kitchen areas are frequently under-sized. Licensed architects designing housing for the National Housing Authority (NHA) or private developers must ensure that even the most compact units meet this 3.00 sq m / 1.50 m minimum. Compliance is not optional regardless of the project's price point.

**Important distinction:** "Kitchen" here means the food preparation space. If a unit has an open-plan layout where the "kitchen" blends into a dining or living area, the Code's minimum still applies to the identifiable kitchen work zone. A pass-through counter in a studio unit does not exempt the kitchen from the minimum area requirement.

### Principle 4: Minimum Bath and Toilet Size — 1.20 sq m, Least Dimension 900 mm

Per PD 1096, Rule VIII, Sec. 806(1)(c), **bath and toilet rooms require a minimum floor area of 1.20 sq m with a least dimension of no less than 900 mm (0.90 m).**

This is the most frequently tested specific number in residential board exam questions. The 1.20 sq m minimum is small — it represents roughly a 1.0 m × 1.2 m footprint, which is the bare minimum needed for a water closet and basin in a Philippine context. The 900 mm least dimension ensures the user can enter, stand, and maneuver without the room being a physical impossibility.

**Practical planning note:** In Philippine residential design, the toilet and bath (T&B) is often one combined room. The 1.20 sq m minimum covers this combined space. If the designer separates the toilet compartment from the bath compartment, each separate space must independently satisfy the minimum — though common sense and the spirit of the Code would require the toilet compartment (at minimum) to meet the 1.20 sq m rule.

**Why 900 mm?** A standard water closet is approximately 350-400 mm wide; clearance in front of the bowl is approximately 500-600 mm. The 900 mm dimension allows for the fixture plus minimum maneuvering clearance. For persons with disabilities (PWD standards under BP 344), the minimum dimensions are much larger (approximately 1.50 m × 1.50 m turning radius), but Section 806 establishes the absolute floor for non-accessible residential design.

### Principle 5: Ceiling Heights — Governed by Rule VIII, Sec. 805

Per PD 1096, Rule VII, Sec. 708(e), ceiling heights for Group A dwellings are governed by **Rule VIII, Sec. 805**. The key provisions of Sec. 805 are:

**For buildings with natural ventilation:**
- Minimum ceiling height: **2.70 m** (floor to ceiling, for all habitable rooms)

**For buildings with artificial/mechanical ventilation:**
- First storey: minimum **2.70 m**
- Second storey: minimum **2.40 m**
- Succeeding storeys (third and above): minimum **2.10 m** (unobstructed head-room clearance)

**For mezzanine floors:**
- Clear ceiling height above and below the mezzanine: not less than **1.80 m**

These ceiling heights reflect the Philippine tropical climate imperative for air circulation. At 2.70 m, a room allows warm air to rise above occupant level, improving thermal comfort in the absence of air conditioning. This is why the 2.70 m minimum is required for naturally ventilated spaces — a lower ceiling in a hot, humid Philippine interior creates a box of trapped hot air that is hazardous to health.

The descending scale for multi-storey buildings with artificial ventilation (2.70 → 2.40 → 2.10) reflects the engineering reality that upper floors in mechanically ventilated buildings can be served by ductwork at lower floor-to-floor heights without sacrificing occupant comfort, since mechanical systems replace the natural convection role of ceiling height.

### Principle 6: Light, Ventilation, and Sanitation Cross-Requirements

Per PD 1096, Rule VII, Sec. 708(b) and (c):

**(b) Light and Ventilation:** Every Group A dwelling must provide adequate light and ventilation per **Sec. 805-811** of Rule VIII. This cross-reference is the formal link between the dwelling requirements of Rule VII and the detailed light/ventilation metrics of Rule VIII.

- Natural ventilation window area: minimum **10% of the floor area** of each room (Sec. 811), with an absolute minimum of **1.00 sq m** regardless of floor area.
- For toilet/bath rooms: window area minimum **1/20 (5%) of floor area**, not less than **240 sq mm**.

**(c) Sanitation:** Every Group A dwelling must have at least:
- **One sanitary toilet**
- **Adequate washing facilities**
- **Adequate drainage facilities**

This minimum sanitation requirement means every Group A dwelling — even a single-room structure — must have a toilet. There is no exception for small structures or temporary use. The "one sanitary toilet" is the absolute minimum; actual household size and BP 344 requirements for larger units may demand more.

### Principle 7: Foundation Requirements — Firm Ground, Adequate Capacity

Per PD 1096, Rule VII, Sec. 708(d), **footings shall be of sufficient size and strength to support the load of the dwelling and shall be built on firm ground.**

While this provision is brief, it carries significant weight in Philippine seismic conditions. The Philippines sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire and experiences frequent earthquakes. "Firm ground" in Philippine practice is interpreted through the National Structural Code of the Philippines (NSCP), which classifies soil types and prescribes foundation depths accordingly. A Group A dwelling built on reclaimed land, soft marine clay, or liquefaction-prone sandy soil requires geotechnical investigation and engineered foundations — the bare requirement of Sec. 708(d) points to this, even if it does not enumerate specific values.

Board exam questions on this provision typically frame the scenario around a dwelling on obviously unsuitable ground (a flood plain, a landslide-prone hillside, reclaimed foreshore land) and ask whether the foundation provision is satisfied. The correct answer invariably invokes the "firm ground" requirement and connects it to the NSCP.

### Principle 8: Section 709 — Requirements for Other Group Occupancies

Per PD 1096, Rule VII, **Sec. 709** extends the principle of minimum occupancy requirements beyond Group A to Groups B through J. While Sec. 709's specific provisions for each group are detailed in the full Code and IRR, the LEA candidate should understand the structural logic:

- **Group A** (Sections 708): Single-family dwellings — the subject of this article.
- **Groups B-J** (Section 709): All other occupancies (residential multi-family, educational, institutional, commercial, industrial, assembly, storage, etc.) have their own minimum requirements, which are generally more stringent in terms of fire resistance, egress, and occupant load calculations.

The principle is hierarchical: Group A (residential, simplest occupancy) has the most permissive minimums. As you move up the occupancy groups, requirements escalate. This hierarchy is a testable concept — knowing that Group A has the most generous minimums compared to other groups helps answer questions about which group triggers a particular requirement first.

|---|---|---|

| **Habitable room — Min area** | **6.00 sq m** (64.6 sq ft) | IRC R304.1: **70 sq ft (6.50 sq m)** minimum; at least one room must be **120 sq ft (11.15 sq m)** |

| **Ceiling height — 2nd storey (mechanical vent)** | **2.40 m** | IBC: **7 ft 6 in (2.29 m)** regardless of storey |
| **Ceiling height — 3rd storey and above (mechanical vent)** | **2.10 m** (headroom clearance) | IBC: **7 ft 6 in (2.29 m)** minimum uniformly; IRC R305.1: corridors/bathrooms 7 ft (2.13 m) |
| **Mezzanine ceiling height** | **1.80 m** above and below | IBC Sec. 505.1: mezzanine headroom minimum **7 ft (2.13 m)** above and below |
| **Natural ventilation window area** | **10% of floor area** (Sec. 811), minimum **1.00 sq m** | IBC Sec. 1203.3: **4% of floor area** for natural ventilation; IRC R303.1: **8% of floor area** for habitable rooms |
| **Bath/toilet ventilation** | Window ≥ **1/20 (5%)** of floor area, min **240 sq mm** | IRC R303.3: mechanical ventilation or window ≥ **1.5 sq ft (0.14 sq m)** openable area |
| **Minimum sanitation** | At least **1 sanitary toilet** + washing + drainage | IRC R306: water closet, lavatory, and bathtub or shower required |
| **Foundation requirement** | Sufficient size/strength; **firm ground** | IBC/IRC: prescriptive foundation depths; geotechnical investigation for problem soils; ASCE 7 load requirements |

**Key Takeaways from the Comparison:**

1. **Philippine lot coverage is dramatically higher than US norms.** The 80-90% maximum lot coverage allowed in the Philippines for residential dwellings is 1.5 to 3 times the typical 30-60% coverage permitted in US residential zoning. This reflects the different land use pressures in densely populated Philippine urban areas versus lower-density US suburban development patterns.

2. **US habitable room minimum is slightly larger.** The IRC's 70 sq ft (6.50 sq m) minimum habitable room is slightly more than the Philippine 6.00 sq m. More significantly, the IRC requires at least one room to be 120 sq ft (11.15 sq m) — a requirement that has no direct equivalent in PD 1096, which sets a uniform 6.00 sq m minimum without a "primary room" larger-room requirement.

3. **Philippine ceiling heights are higher for naturally ventilated spaces.** The Philippine 2.70 m ceiling for naturally ventilated rooms significantly exceeds the IBC's 2.29 m (7'6") and the IRC's 2.13 m (7'0"). This is a deliberate climate-driven design standard — higher ceilings in tropical conditions improve passive cooling and air circulation.

4. **Philippine window area requirement is larger than IBC but smaller than IRC.** PD 1096 requires 10% of floor area in natural ventilation openings. IBC Section 1203 requires only 4% (for commercial buildings). The IRC requires 8% for habitable rooms. PH's 10% reflects the tropical reliance on natural cross-ventilation in the absence of widespread air conditioning.

5. **US provides a mandatory larger room; PH provides uniform minimums.** The IRC R304.1 requirement for at least one 120 sq ft (11.15 sq m) room ensures that even the most compact US dwelling has one genuinely livable space. PD 1096 does not have this "primary room" concept — all habitable rooms are subject to the same 6.00 sq m minimum.

## Cross-Referencing

### Connection to Rule VIII — Ceiling Heights, Room Sizes, Air Space & Ventilation (Sec. 805-811)

Rule VII, Section 708 is explicitly written as a cross-reference document. It mandates compliance with Group A dwelling requirements and then points to Rule VIII for the technical standards. This architecture in the Code's structure is important: **Rule VII tells you WHAT is required; Rule VIII tells you HOW MUCH.**

- Sec. 708(b) → Sec. 805-811 (light and ventilation details)
- Sec. 708(e) → Sec. 806 (room sizes) and Sec. 805 (ceiling heights)

The LEA candidate must be fluent in navigating between these rules. A board question about a Group A dwelling's kitchen minimum may cite Sec. 708 as the source of the requirement but expects you to cite Sec. 806 for the specific dimensions. A question about ceiling height in a Group A bedroom expects Sec. 805 as the answer, not just Sec. 708.

**Air Space Requirement (Sec. 807):** While not directly cited in Sec. 708, the air space per person requirement of Sec. 807 applies to habitable rooms in Group A dwellings. Habitable rooms require **14.00 cubic meters of air space per person.** This is a three-dimensional constraint — if your room meets the 6.00 sq m floor area and 2.70 m ceiling height, it contains 6.00 × 2.70 = 16.20 cu m, which supports one occupant under Sec. 807 (14.00 cu m needed) with minimal margin. A room housing two people would need 28 cu m, requiring either a larger floor area or a higher ceiling.

### Connection to Rule VII — Location on Property (Sec. 704)

Article 11 of this series covered exterior wall fire resistance and opening limitations under Sec. 704. The 2-meter setback from the property line required by Sec. 708(a) interacts with Sec. 704's requirements: a dwelling that is set back 2 meters from the side property line may or may not need fire-rated exterior walls on that side, depending on the Secretary's prescribed fire separation thresholds and the applicable construction type. The setback is a minimum for easement compliance, not a guarantee of no fire-rating requirement.

The lot coverage maximums (80% inside lot, 90% corner lot) also connect to the location rules: a building that maximizes its lot coverage will have minimal unbuilt area around it, which affects both the fire separation distances of Sec. 704 and the available space for the required 2-meter setback. On small lots, the mathematics of coverage percentage + setback minimum can produce a net buildable area much smaller than the headline coverage percentage suggests.

### Connection to Rule V — Fire Zones (Sec. 501-507)

The fire zone designation of the lot determines the allowable construction type for the Group A dwelling. A single-family residence in a Non-Fire Restricted Zone may be built of bamboo, sawali, nipa, and wood (Types I and II Construction). The same dwelling in a Fire Restrictive Zone must meet at least 1-hour fire-resistive construction standards (Types II-IV). In a Highly Fire Restrictive Zone, the house must be Types IV or V Construction — reinforced concrete or structural steel — with fire-resistive exterior walls.

This creates a tiered cost structure for Group A dwellings based on their location. A family in a rural barangay (Non-Fire Restricted Zone) can legally build a nipa hut under PD 1096. A family in a dense urban barangay (Highly Fire Restrictive Zone) must build in concrete and steel. Both are "Group A dwellings" under Rule VII, Sec. 708, but their required construction standards differ radically due to Rule V.

### Connection to BP 344 — Accessibility Law

Batas Pambansa Bilang 344 (Accessibility Law) and its Implementing Rules impose minimum space standards that typically exceed the PD 1096 minimums. For accessible toilet rooms, BP 344 requires a turning radius of approximately 1.50 m × 1.50 m — far larger than the 1.20 sq m minimum of Sec. 806. While BP 344 formally applies to public buildings and facilities, any Group A dwelling that claims accessible design must meet BP 344 standards, which supersede the more permissive PD 1096 minimums for those specific elements.

The LEA candidate should recognize that PD 1096 establishes absolute minimums, not design targets. Professional practice — and compliance with related laws like BP 344 — consistently demands spaces well above these minimums.

### Connection to the Civil Code of the Philippines

Section 708(a) explicitly states the 2-meter setback is "subject to Civil Code easements of light and view." The Civil Code's Articles 667-673 establish the right of an adjoining property owner to light and view, including the prohibition against openings in walls directly on the property boundary and the required minimum distances for windows looking into neighboring property. These Civil Code provisions operate as an **independent legal constraint** on top of the building code requirements.

A wall built exactly 2.0 m from the property line may comply with Sec. 708(a) but still violate Civil Code Article 670, which requires windows in a wall less than 3 meters from the boundary to be equipped with a fixed iron grating and wire screen to protect the neighbor's privacy. The architect must satisfy both bodies of law simultaneously.

### Connection to NSCP (National Structural Code of the Philippines)

The foundation requirement of Sec. 708(d) — "firm ground" and "sufficient size and strength" — is technically implemented through the NSCP, which provides the engineering standards for soil bearing capacity, foundation depth, and seismic design requirements. In a country with the Philippines' seismic and volcanic hazard profile, "firm ground" is a loaded phrase. The NSCP classifies soil into Site Classes (from rock to soft clay) and mandates different foundation depths and types for each. Compliance with Sec. 708(d) requires, at a minimum, knowledge of NSCP foundation provisions and, in many cases, geotechnical investigation reports.

## Mnemonic Devices

### Mnemonic 1: "6-3-1.2" — The Three Room Minimums, In Order

> **6** — Habitable room minimum: **6.00 sq m**
> **3** — Kitchen minimum: **3.00 sq m**
> **1.2** — Bath/Toilet minimum: **1.20 sq m**

Read it as a descending sequence: six, three, one-point-two. Each number is exactly half the previous one (6 → 3 → 1.5... close enough for memory purposes, given 1.20 ≈ 40% of 3). This sequence is easy to recall because it counts down by roughly halving. Pair each number with its minimum least dimension: **2.00 m / 1.50 m / 900 mm.**

Combined recall chain: **"6 by 2, 3 by 1.5, 1.2 by 0.9"** — habitable, kitchen, toilet. Once you drill this sequence, no board question on room minimums will catch you off guard.

### Mnemonic 2: "CLOCK" — What a Group A Dwelling Must Have

> **C** — **Coverage** limited (90% corner / 80% inside lot)
> **L** — **Light and ventilation** per Sec. 805-811
> **O** — **One sanitary toilet** minimum (plus washing + drainage)
> **C** — **Ceiling heights** per Sec. 805 (2.70 / 2.40 / 2.10)
> **K** — **Kind of ground** must be firm; foundations must support loads

"CLOCK" captures the five substantive requirements of Sec. 708: coverage, light/ventilation, one toilet, ceiling heights, and kind-of-ground (foundation on firm ground). A dwelling that passes the CLOCK checklist satisfies the core structure of Sec. 708.

## Exam Trap Learts

**TRAP 1:** "A habitable room that is 3.0 m × 2.0 m = 6.0 sq m satisfies the minimum requirements for a Group A dwelling bedroom."

**TRUTH:** The area check (6.00 sq m) is satisfied, but you must also verify the least-dimension check. A 3.0 m × 2.0 m room has a least dimension of **2.00 m** — which exactly meets the 2.00 m minimum. So this room actually **does** comply, but only barely. The trap version of this question often presents a 4.0 m × 1.5 m room (6.00 sq m area, but least dimension 1.5 m < 2.00 m required) — that room fails. Both conditions must be met: **area AND least dimension.** Never apply just one criterion.

---

**TRAP 2:** "The minimum ceiling height for a Group A dwelling bedroom is 2.40 m, as stated in Section 805."

**TRUTH:** The 2.40 m minimum applies specifically to the **second storey** of a multi-storey building with **artificial ventilation** (mechanical/air conditioning). For a naturally ventilated room — the default in a simple Group A dwelling — the minimum ceiling height is **2.70 m** per Sec. 805. Board exams frequently offer 2.40 m as an answer option knowing that candidates confuse it with the general minimum. The 2.40 m figure is correct only in a specific context (second storey, artificial ventilation). For a typical naturally ventilated house, 2.70 m is the answer.

---

**TRAP 3:** "A Group A dwelling on a 100 sq m inside lot can have a building footprint of 80 sq m (80% lot coverage) and be placed anywhere on the lot."

**TRUTH:** The 80% maximum lot coverage means the footprint cannot exceed 80 sq m. However, Sec. 708(a) additionally requires the dwelling to be **at least 2 meters from the property line** (subject to Civil Code easements of light and view). On a 100 sq m inside lot (e.g., 8 m wide × 12.5 m deep), the 2-meter setback on all sides reduces the buildable footprint to (8 − 4) × (12.5 − 4) = 4 m × 8.5 m = **34 sq m** — far less than the 80 sq m coverage maximum. The two requirements (coverage limit and setback minimum) are independent constraints; the more restrictive one governs. Exam questions that present only the coverage percentage and ask for the maximum footprint are trapping candidates who ignore the setback.

## Active Recall Questions

**Question 1**

A licensed architect is designing a single-family dwelling on a 120 sq m inside lot in a suburban barangay. The client wants to maximize the building footprint. Per PD 1096, Rule VII, Sec. 708(a), what is the maximum lot coverage allowed for this dwelling?

- A. 72 sq m (60% of 120 sq m)
- B. 84 sq m (70% of 120 sq m)
- C. 96 sq m (80% of 120 sq m)
- D. 108 sq m (90% of 120 sq m)

> **Answer: C — 96 sq m (80% of 120 sq m)**
>
<Note>

Per PD 1096, Rule VII, Sec. 708(a), a Group A dwelling on an inside lot shall occupy not more than 80% of the lot area. 120 sq m × 80% = 96 sq m. The 90% coverage (Option D) applies to corner lots, not inside lots. Option A (60%) and Option B (70%) have no basis in Sec. 708. The candidate must distinguish between corner lot (90%) and inside lot (80%) — this distinction is the primary exam test point in this provision. Note also that the 2-meter setback requirement may further reduce the achievable footprint below 96 sq m depending on lot dimensions.

</Note>
>
<LawCallout code="pd1096" section="Rule VII - Group A - Dwellings">


LEA Area: Building Technology — National Building Code of the Philippines


</LawCallout>

---

**Question 2**

Per PD 1096, which of the following correctly describes the minimum dimensions for a kitchen in a Group A dwelling?

- A. Minimum 6.00 sq m with a least dimension of 2.00 m
- B. Minimum 3.00 sq m with a least dimension of 1.50 m
- C. Minimum 3.00 sq m with a least dimension of 1.00 m
- D. Minimum 1.20 sq m with a least dimension of 900 mm

> **Answer: B — Minimum 3.00 sq m with a least dimension of 1.50 m**
>
<LawCallout code="pd1096" section="Rule VII - Minimum Requirements">


Per PD 1096, Rule VIII, Sec. 806(1)(b), invoked by Rule VII, Sec. 708(e): kitchens require a minimum floor area of 3.00 sq m and a least dimension of 1.50 m. Option A describes habitable rooms (Sec. 806(1)(a)), not kitchens. Option C has the correct area but an incorrect least dimension (1.00 m is too small). Option D describes the bath and toilet room (Sec. 806(1)(c)). Board exams routinely offer all three room types as distractors for each other — knowing the specific numbers for each room type is essential.


</LawCallout>
>
<LawCallout code="pd1096" section="Rule VII - Room Dimensions">


LEA Area: Building Technology — National Building Code of the Philippines


</LawCallout>

---

**Question 3**

A developer is constructing a two-storey Group A dwelling with mechanical air conditioning throughout. Per PD 1096, Rule VIII, Sec. 805, what are the minimum ceiling heights required for the first and second storeys, respectively?

- A. First storey: 2.40 m; Second storey: 2.10 m
- B. First storey: 2.70 m; Second storey: 2.10 m
- C. First storey: 2.70 m; Second storey: 2.40 m
- D. First storey: 2.40 m; Second storey: 2.40 m

> **Answer: C — First storey: 2.70 m; Second storey: 2.40 m**
>
<LawCallout code="pd1096" section="Rule VII - Ceiling Heights">


Per PD 1096, Rule VIII, Sec. 805, for buildings with artificial ventilation: first storey minimum = 2.70 m; second storey minimum = 2.40 m; succeeding storeys = minimum 2.10 m unobstructed headroom clearance. This is one of the most exam-tested provisions in Rule VIII. Option A is wrong on both storeys (first storey must be 2.70 m, not 2.40 m). Option B has the first storey correct but applies the third-storey clearance (2.10 m) to the second. Option D applies 2.40 m to the first storey, which is incorrect — first storey must be 2.70 m regardless of ventilation type. The first storey standard (2.70 m) applies equally to naturally and artificially ventilated buildings; only the second storey gets the reduced 2.40 m allowance.


</LawCallout>
>
<LawCallout code="pd1096" section="Rule VIII - Light and Ventilation">


LEA Area: Building Technology — National Building Code of the Philippines


</LawCallout>

---



---

## Cross‑References

**Residential Clearances**, **Ceiling Heights And Room Sizes**, **Pd 1096 Rule Vii Occupancy**, **Lodging And Residential Accessibility**

## Verified Sources

- **PD 1096** — National Building Code of the Philippines (Presidential Decree No. 1096, 1977)
- **2004 Revised Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) of PD 1096** — Rule VII, Section 708 (Minimum Requirements for Group A Dwellings); Rule VII, Section 709 (Requirements for Other Group Occupancies); Rule VIII, Section 805 (Ceiling Heights); Rule VIII, Section 806 (Sizes and Dimensions of Rooms); Rule VIII, Section 807 (Air Space Requirements); Rule VIII, Section 811 (Artificial Ventilation); Rule V, Sections 501-507 (Fire Zones); Rule VII, Section 704 (Location on Property — cross-reference to Article 11)
- **IRC 2021** — International Residential Code, Section R304 (Minimum Room Areas), Section R305 (Ceiling Height), Section R306 (Sanitation), Section R307 (Toilet, Bath, and Shower Spaces)
- **IBC 2021** — International Building Code, Section 1208 (Interior Space Dimensions), Section 1203 (Ventilation), Section 505 (Mezzanines)
- **ASHRAE 62.1** — Ventilation for Acceptable Indoor Air Quality (commercial buildings)
- **ASHRAE 62.2** — Ventilation and Acceptable Indoor Air Quality in Residential Buildings
- **Architectural Graphic Standards** (Ramsey/Sleeper, 12th Ed.) — Chapter on Residential Design; kitchen and bath dimension guidelines; room planning standards
- **Metric Handbook: Planning and Design Data** (Littlefield, ed.) — Residential space standards; ceiling height recommendations for tropical climates; room dimension guidelines
- **Civil Code of the Philippines** — Articles 667-673 (Easements of Light and View); relevant to the 2-meter setback and window limitations at property boundaries
- **Batas Pambansa Bilang 344** — Accessibility Law of the Philippines and its Implementing Rules; minimum toilet room dimensions for accessible design (supersede PD 1096 minimums for accessible elements)
- **National Structural Code of the Philippines (NSCP)** — Foundation requirements, soil classification, and seismic design standards; implements the "firm ground" requirement of Sec. 708(d)
- **National Housing Authority (NHA) Standards** — Minimum dwelling unit standards for socialized and economic housing in the Philippines (implementing agency guidelines for Group A dwellings in government housing programs)
