rows.title: Lathing and Plastering
rows.content:
# Lathing and Plastering
## Learning Goal

After reading this article, you should be able to:

Identify the materials, thicknesses, and application methods for lath and plaster construction under PD 1096 Rule XVI; distinguish metal lath, gypsum lath, and wire lath by fire-resistance rating; apply the minimum plaster thickness for fire-rated assemblies; and determine when lath-and-plaster is an acceptable fire-resistive covering.
---

## 1. Hook / Opening Scenario

You are reviewing construction documents for a five-storey Type IV (steel frame) commercial building in Quezon City. The plans specify 9.5 mm standard gypsum board on corridor walls — the walls separating tenant spaces from the means of egress. You know the corridor must be fire-rated. You reach for your red pen. This is exactly the kind of call the LEA board exam asks you to make: knowing which wall board, in which thickness, satisfies both the type of construction and the fire-resistive rating required by the National Building Code.

---

<LawCallout code="nbcp">

Rule XII, Sec. 1215: Lath, plaster, and gypsum wall board must conform to both (a) fire-resistive rating requirements under Rule VI and (b) type of construction under Rule IV. The days of merely referencing 'Secretary's standards' are over — the IRR gives specific cross-references.

</LawCallout>

<Warn>

⚠️ Common Error: 9.5 mm standard gypsum board is NOT fire-rated. For corridor walls requiring fire-resistive rating, you need Type X (15.9 mm or 12.7 mm) gypsum board. Standard gypsum board on a corridor separating tenant space from means of egress will fail inspection.

</Warn>

<ExamTip>

LEA Pattern: Questions test the relationship between type of construction (Type I-V) and required wall board. Type IV steel frame requires 12.7 mm Type X gypsum board for 1-hour rated corridors. Type V wood frame may use 15.9 mm Type X for same rating. Match the type to the thickness.

</ExamTip>

## 2. Core Concepts with Mnemonic

### The Governing Provision

**PD 1096, Section 1215 (Basic Law, 1977):**
> "The installation of lath, plaster and gypsum wall board shall conform to the fire-resistive requirements as set forth by the Secretary."

**2004 Revised IRR, Rule XII, Section 1215:**
> "The installation of lath, plaster and gypsum wall board shall conform to the fire-resistive rating requirements and the type of construction of building."

**What changed:** The IRR is more specific — it ties installation requirements to both (a) the fire-resistive rating requirements under Rule VI and (b) the type of construction under Rule IV. The basic law delegated to the Secretary of Public Works; the IRR operationalizes that delegation by pointing to the existing rules framework.

---

### The Five Key Principles of Section 1215

**Principle 1 — Type of Construction Governs Material Selection**
The type of construction (Types I–V, per PD 1096, Rule IV) determines whether lath, plaster, and wall board must be combustible, limited-combustible, or incombustible. A Type V (fire-resistive) building cannot use wood lath. A Type I (wood frame) building has no fire-resistive requirements for interior partitions but is still subject to fire zone restrictions.

**Principle 2 — Fire-Resistive Ratings Are Non-Negotiable at Key Locations**
Per the 2004 Revised IRR, Rule VI (Fire-Resistive Standards), certain building elements must achieve tested fire-resistance ratings regardless of the occupancy group or construction type when code mandates them (e.g., corridor walls, shaft walls, stairwell enclosures). The wall board or plaster assembly must be part of a rated assembly — not just a single product specification.

**Principle 3 — It Is an Assembly, Not a Single Product**
No single product achieves a fire-resistance rating in isolation. A 15.9 mm (5/8") Type X gypsum board achieves a 1-hour rating only when installed as part of a complete tested assembly: the correct stud size and spacing, fastener pattern, joint treatment, and any required insulation. Per ASTM C840 and UL-listed assemblies, deviation from the assembly specification voids the rating.

**Principle 4 — Plaster Thickness and Application Method Are Prescribed**
Plaster thickness requirements are prescribed by material type and substrate. The three-coat system (scratch coat → brown coat → finish coat) is required over metal lath. The two-coat system is permitted over gypsum lath. Exterior cement plaster is not interchangeable with interior gypsum plaster; using the wrong plaster type in the wrong environment causes premature failure.

**Principle 5 — Philippine Practice Anchors on CHB + Plaster, but Drywall Is Growing**
The dominant Philippine wall system — concrete hollow block (CHB) with cement plaster finish — inherently satisfies fire-resistive requirements for most types of construction due to the incombustibility of masonry. Gypsum board (drywall) partitions are common in commercial fit-outs; these require careful specification of the board type, thickness, and assembly to meet fire-rating requirements.

---

### Primary Mnemonic: **"FLAT-CF"** — The Six Decision Points for Wall Board Selection

| Letter | Decision Point |
|--------|---------------|
| **F** | **Fire-resistive rating required?** (Corridor, shaft, stair, or occupancy separation) |
| **L** | **Location** — interior or exterior; wet or dry |
| **A** | **Assembly** — is it a tested/rated assembly or non-rated partition? |
| **T** | **Type of construction** — combustible, limited, or incombustible allowed? |
| **C** | **Code reference** — what does Rule VI, RA 9514, or the referral standard require? |
| **F** | **Finish** — flame-spread requirements for interior finish (RA 9514, Fire Code) |

Use **FLAT-CF** every time you specify or review a wall board specification.

---

## 3. Hard Data Tables (Cheat Sheet)

### Table 3.1 — Types of Lath: Properties and Code Limitations

| Lath Type | Description | Permitted in Type I | Permitted in Types II–V | Key Philippine Use |
|-----------|-------------|--------------------|--------------------------|--------------------|
| Wood lath | Thin wood strips, nailed to studs | Yes | No (combustible) | Rare; legacy residential |
| Gypsum lath | Paper-faced gypsum board, 9.5–12.7 mm | Yes | Yes (non-structural) | Commercial ceilings |
| Metal lath — expanded | Diamond mesh, minimum 2.4 kg/m² (walls) | Yes | Yes | Exterior plaster, fire-rated |
| Metal lath — woven wire | Galvanized wire mesh | Yes | Yes | Exterior stucco |
| Metal lath — welded wire | Rigid galvanized grid | Yes | Yes | Precast wall panels |

> **IBC Reference (IBC 2510):** Metal lath minimum weight — 1.36 kg/m² (2.5 lb/sq.yd) for walls, 1.85 kg/m² (3.4 lb/sq.yd) for ceilings and soffits.

---

### Table 3.2 — Plaster Types: Properties, Applications, and Mix Ratios

| Plaster Type | Base | Interior/Exterior | Wet Areas | Typical Mix Ratio | Coats Required | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Portland cement plaster (stucco) | Cement | Both | Yes | 1:3 to 1:4 (cement:sand) | 3 (over metal lath) | Dominant exterior finish in PH |
| Gypsum plaster | Gypsum | Interior only | No | Pre-mixed or 1:2 | 2–3 | NOT for wet or exterior |
| Lime plaster | Lime putty | Interior only | No | 1:2–3 (lime:sand) | 3 | Sets by carbonation; slow |
| Keene's cement | Burnt gypsum + alum | Interior only | Humid (not wet) | Factory mix | 2 | Hard, dense finish coat |

<Note>

PH Practice Note: Portland cement plaster on CHB at 15–20 mm exterior / 12–15 mm interior is the standard Philippine specification. Gypsum plaster is used in commercial interiors where faster setting and smoother finish are required.

</Note>

---

### Table 3.3 — Gypsum Wall Board: Types, Thicknesses, and Applications

| Board Type | Common Name | Standard Thickness | Application | Fire Rating Contribution | Philippine Availability |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Regular (Type R) | Plain drywall | 9.5 mm, 12.7 mm | Non-rated interior partitions | None per se | Common (commercial) |
| Type X | Fire-rated | 15.9 mm (5/8") | 1-hour rated assemblies | Part of 1-hr assembly | Widely available |
| Type C | Enhanced fire-rated | 15.9 mm | Better fire performance | Exceeds Type X | Specialty import |
| Moisture-resistant (MR) | Green board | 12.7 mm, 15.9 mm | Humid areas (NOT wet) | None specifically | Common (commercial) |
| Cement board | Backer board | 9.5 mm, 12.7 mm | Tile substrate, wet areas | Limited | Common (hardware) |
| Abuse-resistant | AR board | 15.9 mm | High-traffic corridors | May incorporate Type X | Specialty |

> **Key Metric Conversion:** 1/2" = 12.7 mm | 5/8" = 15.9 mm | 3/8" = 9.5 mm

---

### Table 3.4 — Fire-Resistive Requirements by Type of Construction (PD 1096, Rule IV & Rule VI)

| Type of Construction | Description | Interior Partitions (Non-Bearing) | Bearing Walls | Permitted Lath/Board |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Type I | Combustible (wood frame) | None required | None required | Wood lath, gypsum board, metal lath |
| Type II | Wood + fire protection | 1-hour fire-resistive | 1-hour fire-resistive | Gypsum board (Type X or assembly), metal lath + plaster |
| Type III | Masonry exterior + wood interior | 1-hour fire-resistive | Masonry (non-rated) | Gypsum board (Type X), metal lath + plaster |
| Type IV | Steel/concrete frame | Incombustible; 1-hour for non-bearing | Incombustible | Type X gypsum board, cement board, metal lath + plaster |
| Type V | Fire-resistive throughout | 2-hour or per fire-resistive design | 2–4 hour fire-resistive | Metal lath + plaster (rated); Type X in tested assemblies |

---

### Table 3.5 — Plaster Coat Thickness Requirements: PH Practice vs. IBC

| System | Coat | Over Metal Lath (mm) | Over Gypsum Lath (mm) | Over Masonry/CHB (mm) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3-coat (cement) | Scratch coat | 9–10 | N/A | 9–10 |
| 3-coat (cement) | Brown coat | 10–12 | N/A | 10–12 |
| 3-coat (cement) | Finish coat | 3–5 | N/A | 3–5 |
| **Total (3-coat)** | — | **22–27 mm** | N/A | **22–27 mm** |
| 2-coat (gypsum) | Base coat | 8–10 | 6–8 | N/A |
| 2-coat (gypsum) | Finish coat | 3–5 | 3–5 | N/A |
| **Total (2-coat)** | — | **11–15 mm** | **9–13 mm** | N/A |
| PH exterior stucco | All coats | 15–20 mm typical | N/A | 15–20 mm typical |
| PH interior plaster | All coats | 12–15 mm typical | N/A | 12–15 mm typical |

> **IBC 2508.1 Reference:** Minimum 3-coat exterior Portland cement plaster over metal lath = 22 mm (7/8") total.

---

### Table 3.6 — PH vs. USA Standards Quick Reference

| Parameter | PH Standard (PD 1096 / 2004 IRR) | USA Standard (IBC 2021) |
|---|---|---|
| Governing provision | Rule XII, Section 1215 | IBC Chapter 25 |
| Fire-rating determination | Rule VI + Type of Construction (Rule IV) | IBC Chapter 7 + UL assemblies |
| Gypsum board standard | References referral codes (ASTM) | ASTM C1396 / C36 |
| Installation standard | References referral codes | ASTM C840 (interior), ASTM C926 (plaster) |
| Gypsum board association manual | Not cited explicitly in code | GA-216 Fire-Resistance Design Manual |
| Metal lath weight — walls | Not specified independently; per referral standards | Min. 1.36 kg/m² (IBC 2510) |
| Metal lath weight — ceilings | Per referral standards | Min. 1.85 kg/m² (IBC 2510) |
| Type X board thickness | 15.9 mm (by industry standard) | 15.9 mm (IBC 2506.2) |
| Exterior plaster total thickness | 15–20 mm (PH practice) | Min. 22 mm / 7/8" (IBC 2508.1) |
| Interior cement plaster restriction | Per referral codes | No calcium sulfate (IBC 2511.3) |
| Dominant exterior wall system | CHB + cement plaster | Stud framing + sheathing + veneer |

---

## 4. In-Depth Technical Analysis

### 4.1 The Legislative Structure Behind Section 1215

Section 1215 is one of the shortest provisions in PD 1096, occupying a single sentence in the basic law. Its brevity is intentional: the original law delegates technical content to standards set by the Secretary of the DPWH. The 2004 Revised IRR fills this delegation by directing practitioners to Rules IV and VI — creating a cross-referencing framework rather than restating technical standards within Section 1215 itself.

This legislative structure has a critical implication for the LEA examination: **Section 1215 is not a standalone provision.** It is the connector between the fire-resistive framework (Rule VI), the construction type framework (Rule IV), and the actual installation of wall finishes. Exam questions on this section will frequently test your ability to trace that connection.

### 4.2 Types of Lath in Detail

**Metal Lath** is the most important lath type for fire-rated construction in the Philippines. Expanded metal lath (diamond mesh) is the most common form, produced by slitting and expanding a metal sheet. It provides mechanical keying for plaster adhesion and forms part of fire-rated plaster assemblies.

- **Weight classification:** Standard weight for wall applications is approximately 2.4 kg/m²; heavier lath is used for ceiling and soffit work where the plaster must bond overhead.
- **Corrosion protection:** Galvanized or painted; critical in the Philippine coastal and humid environment.
- **Fire performance:** Metal lath with three-coat Portland cement plaster over steel studs can achieve a 1-hour fire-resistance rating when the assembly conforms to an ASTM or UL-tested design.

**Gypsum Lath (Rocklath)** consists of a core of gypsum plaster with a paper facing that provides mechanical bond for finish plaster coats. At 9.5–12.7 mm thickness, it is lighter than solid gypsum wall board and is used primarily as a plaster base for two-coat plaster systems. It is suitable for Types I through V construction when used as part of a tested, rated assembly.

**Wood Lath** is historical. In the Philippine context, wood lath is classified as combustible and is incompatible with fire-resistive requirements. It may appear in pre-code residential construction but should not be specified for any new work where fire-resistive construction is required. Per PD 1096, Rule IV, it is appropriate only in Type I (combustible) construction and is not permitted where fire-resistive ratings must be achieved.

### 4.3 Plaster Systems in Detail

**Three-Coat System (Over Metal Lath)**

This is the standard exterior plaster application and the required system for metal lath substrates:

1. **Scratch coat** — Applied immediately after lath installation. The wet plaster is forced through the mesh openings to create a mechanical key. While still wet, it is scratched (scored) to provide a rough surface for the brown coat. Typical thickness: 9–10 mm.

2. **Brown coat** — Applied after the scratch coat has cured (minimum 48 hours for cement plaster). This is the leveling coat; it brings the surface to a true, flat plane. Thickness: 10–12 mm. The brown coat must be damp-cured for Portland cement plasters to prevent premature drying and cracking.

3. **Finish coat** — The final surface coat, applied thin (3–5 mm) over a dampened brown coat. For exterior: sand finish or textured. For interior: smooth finish (gypsum putty or lime-based) or texture.

**Two-Coat System (Over Gypsum Lath or Masonry)**

On gypsum lath or smooth masonry, a scratch coat is not required because mechanical keying is provided by the substrate surface or paper facing:
1. **Base coat** — Single leveling coat, 6–10 mm depending on substrate.
2. **Finish coat** — Same as three-coat system, 3–5 mm.

**Material Compatibility Rules:**

| Rule | Rationale |
|------|-----------|
| Gypsum plaster = interior only | Gypsum is water-soluble; exterior exposure causes dissolution and failure |
| Portland cement plaster = exterior and wet areas | Cement cures by hydration; moisture-resistant after full cure |
| No calcium sulfate in interior cement plaster | Calcium sulfate interferes with cement hydration (per IBC 2511.3, adopted as referral standard) |
| Lime plaster over masonry | Lime is compatible with masonry chemistry (both alkaline); adhesion is excellent |

### 4.4 Gypsum Wall Board Systems in Detail

**Standard (Type R) Gypsum Board**

Regular gypsum board consists of a gypsum plaster core encased in paper facings. The gypsum core is non-combustible and slows heat transmission, but standard board without additives does not achieve tested fire-resistance ratings on its own. It is appropriate for non-rated interior partitions in Types I through V construction.

**Type X Gypsum Board (Fire-Rated)**

Type X board contains glass fibers and other additives distributed throughout the gypsum core that reinforce the board during fire exposure and inhibit shrinkage. At 15.9 mm thickness, a tested assembly using Type X board on steel studs typically achieves 1-hour fire-resistance rating per ASTM E119 or the equivalent UL assembly.

Critical characteristics:
- Must be labeled "Type X" or "Fire-Rated" by the manufacturer
- The rating belongs to the assembly, not the board alone
- Double-layer applications (two layers of 15.9 mm Type X) can achieve 2-hour ratings in tested assemblies
- Per the 2004 Revised IRR cross-reference to Rule VI and referral codes, any claim of fire resistance must be backed by a tested assembly

**Type C Gypsum Board**

Type C board is an enhanced formulation beyond Type X. It typically contains more glass fibers and special additives that allow the board to maintain its integrity longer under fire exposure. While not explicitly defined in PD 1096, Type C boards are specified in fire-rated assemblies under the referral standards framework. They are particularly useful in lightweight steel-frame construction.

**Moisture-Resistant Board (Green Board)**

MR board has a water-resistant paper facing and moisture-resistant additives in the core. It is appropriate for areas with elevated humidity (e.g., behind kitchen cabinetry, in laundry rooms) but is explicitly NOT appropriate for direct water contact or as a direct tile substrate in shower enclosures. In the Philippine context, a common error is specifying green board in toilet and bath tile areas — the correct substrate is cement board.

**Cement Board**

Cement board (e.g., HardieBacker, Durock, and locally available equivalents) is a cementitious panel with fiberglass reinforcement. It is the correct substrate for tile in wet areas (bathrooms, shower enclosures, kitchen splash areas) because it is dimensionally stable when wet and does not support mold growth. It is not a fire-rated product per se, but it is incombustible.

### 4.5 Installation Requirements for Gypsum Board

The following installation principles apply in Philippine practice under the referral standards framework:

**Framing and Fastening:**
- Steel studs at 400 mm or 600 mm on center (standard spacing for rated assemblies — deviation voids the rating)
- Screws at 200–300 mm on center at field; 150–200 mm at edges for rated assemblies
- Board joints must be staggered between layers in multi-layer assemblies
- Gypsum board must not touch the floor slab — maintain a 10–12 mm gap to prevent moisture wicking

**Joint Treatment:**
- All joints, fasteners, and corners must be taped and compounded to complete the rated assembly
- Untreated joints represent gaps in the fire barrier and void the tested assembly

**Penetrations:**
- All penetrations through rated assemblies (pipes, conduits, cables) must be protected with UL-listed firestopping systems per Rule VI and RA 9514

**Grab Bar Blocking (BP 344):**
- Where grab bars are required per BP 344 (Accessibility Law), solid wood or steel blocking must be installed within the wall cavity at the correct height to provide a substrate for fastening — gypsum board alone will not support the required loads

### 4.6 Fire-Resistive Construction and the Role of Wall Finishes

The fire-resistive rating of a wall assembly is achieved through the combined thermal resistance of all components: the framing, insulation (if any), the board layers, and the joint treatment. Section 1215 is best understood as the code's recognition that the interior finish layer is not cosmetic — it is a structural component of the fire barrier.

**At corridor walls** (Rule XII, Section 1207): A 1-hour fire-resistive rating is required for corridor walls in most occupancy groups. This means the gypsum board type, thickness, fastener pattern, stud spacing, and joint treatment must all conform to a tested 1-hour assembly. Specifying 12.7 mm (1/2") standard board on a corridor wall fails this requirement.

**At shaft walls** (Rule XII, Section 1204): Elevator, mechanical, and plumbing shafts must be enclosed in rated construction. Shaft wall assemblies use special gypsum liner panels (often 25 mm / 1" thick) designed for one-sided installation into the shaft without interior access.

**At exit stairways:** Stair enclosure walls require fire-resistive construction per Rule XII and Rule VI. Metal lath and Portland cement plaster or tested gypsum board assemblies are used.

---

## 5. PH vs. USA Comparative Analysis

### 5.1 Structure of the Code

The fundamental difference is one of **specificity vs. framework**:

- **PD 1096 / IRR (PH):** Section 1215 is a one-sentence provision that delegates all technical content to (a) the type of construction rules, (b) the fire-resistive standards, and (c) referral codes adopted by the DPWH Secretary. The IRR does not reproduce ASTM standards or UL assembly numbers. Practitioners must cross-reference to the referral code library.

- **IBC (USA):** Chapter 25 is a detailed standalone chapter with specific provisions on gypsum board thickness (Section 2506), lath weight (Section 2510), plaster coat thickness (Section 2508), specific prohibitions (Section 2511.3 — no calcium sulfate in interior cement plaster), and explicit cross-references to ASTM standards for each material.

**Implication for LEA Candidates:** Philippine code on this topic is a framework, not a recipe book. On the exam, you will be tested on the framework (which rule governs? what type of construction? what fire-resistive rating is required?) rather than memorized ASTM tables.

### 5.2 Material Specifications

| Specification | PH Standard | USA Standard (IBC) | More Restrictive |
|---|---|---|---|
| Exterior plaster total thickness | 15–20 mm (practice) | 22 mm minimum (IBC 2508.1) | USA |
| Metal lath — walls | Per referral standard | Min. 1.36 kg/m² (IBC 2510) | USA (explicit) |
| Metal lath — ceilings | Per referral standard | Min. 1.85 kg/m² (IBC 2510) | USA (explicit) |
| 1-hour corridor wall assembly | 15.9 mm Type X in rated assembly | 15.9 mm Type X in tested assembly | equivalent |
| Green board in wet areas | Not explicitly prohibited in code text; standard practice prohibits | Not permitted as direct tile substrate | equivalent (practice) |
| Fire-rating verification | Assembly conformance (referral codes) | UL assembly listing required | USA (more prescriptive) |
| Wood lath in Types II–V | Prohibited (combustible) | Prohibited by fire-resistive requirements | equivalent |

### 5.3 Philippine Construction Context

The Philippine building industry differs from the US in several ways that affect how Section 1215 is applied in practice:

1. **CHB dominance:** In the Philippines, masonry walls (CHB + cement plaster) are the default. This system is inherently incombustible and meets fire-resistive requirements without reference to tested drywall assemblies. The Section 1215 framework matters most for the growing commercial drywall market.

2. **Tropical climate:** High humidity and the presence of coastal salt air accelerate corrosion of steel lath and studs. Galvanized or stainless-steel framing is essential, particularly near the coast. Gypsum board in high-humidity environments without proper air conditioning requires moisture-resistant board as minimum.

3. **Seismic conditions:** The Philippines is in a high-seismic zone. Gypsum board partitions must accommodate seismic drift — steel stud systems must be detailed with sufficient clearance at the top track (typically 25–38 mm) so that the partition does not carry vertical load during seismic movement. This is a structural detail, not a Section 1215 issue per se, but it affects wall board installation.

4. **Fire zone requirements (Rule V):** Buildings in Fire Zone 1 face additional restrictions. In Zone 1, exterior wall finishes must be non-combustible, which further restricts the use of certain lath and plaster systems.

---

## 6. Exam Traps

### Trap 1 — "Any Gypsum Board Satisfies a 1-Hour Rating"

**Wrong answer:** A 12.7 mm (1/2") standard gypsum board on steel studs provides a 1-hour fire-resistance rating.

**Why it's wrong:** Fire-resistance ratings belong to assemblies, not individual products. Standard (Type R) gypsum board does not achieve a 1-hour rating regardless of thickness. A 1-hour rated assembly requires, at minimum, 15.9 mm (5/8") **Type X** board with the correct stud spacing, fastener pattern, and joint treatment — all as part of a tested assembly per ASTM E119 or an equivalent protocol.

**Correct answer:** The 1-hour rated assembly must conform to a tested design using Type X gypsum board (15.9 mm) installed per the assembly specification. Per the 2004 Revised IRR, Rule XII, Section 1215, the installation must conform to fire-resistive rating requirements — meaning the entire assembly must be rated, not just one component.

---

### Trap 2 — "Gypsum Plaster Can Be Used Anywhere Plaster Is Required"

**Wrong answer:** Specifying gypsum plaster for the exterior facade of a building satisfies the plaster requirement of Section 1215.

**Why it's wrong:** Gypsum plaster is **interior-only**. Gypsum is water-soluble and will dissolve, crack, and fail when exposed to weather. Philippine tropical conditions — high humidity, heavy rainfall, and direct sun — make exterior gypsum plaster wholly inappropriate. The correct exterior plaster is Portland cement plaster (stucco), which cures by hydration and becomes moisture-resistant.

**Correct answer:** Portland cement plaster, mixed at 1:3 to 1:4 (cement:sand), applied in a three-coat system over metal lath, is the correct specification for exterior plaster. Gypsum plaster is limited to interior, dry areas only.

---

### Trap 3 — "Type of Construction Doesn't Affect Wall Board Thickness"

**Wrong answer:** Because Section 1215 is a brief provision, wall board thickness is a matter of architect's choice and is not affected by the type of construction.

**Why it's wrong:** The 2004 Revised IRR explicitly ties Section 1215 to the fire-resistive rating requirements *and* the type of construction. In a Type IV or Type V building, partitions that require fire-resistive ratings must use tested assemblies with Type X (or better) gypsum board. The type of construction determines whether fire-resistive ratings are required for a given building element; once a rating is required, the assembly (including board thickness and type) is fixed by the tested design.

**Correct answer:** Per the 2004 Revised IRR, Rule XII, Section 1215, installation must conform to both the fire-resistive rating requirements (Rule VI) and the type of construction (Rule IV). The type of construction directly determines whether a fire-rated assembly is required, which in turn determines the board type and thickness.

---

## 7. Board-Prep Mnemonics

### Mnemonic 1: **"SMOKE"** — Five Things That Determine Your Wall Board Spec

> **S** — **Site location** (exterior or interior; wet or dry)
> **M** — **Material type permitted** by type of construction (combustible or incombustible)
> **O** — **Opening/Assembly** — is it a rated assembly or a non-rated partition?
> **K** — **Key code requirements** — Rule IV, Rule VI, RA 9514 flame spread, BP 344 blocking
> **E** — **Environment** — tropical humidity, seismic drift gap, corrosion of framing

Every gypsum board spec decision runs through SMOKE. Get one wrong and the wall fails — on site or on the exam.

---

### Mnemonic 2: **"SBF"** — The Three-Coat Plaster Sequence

> **S** — **Scratch coat** (mechanical key; scratched while wet)
> **B** — **Brown coat** (bulk; leveling coat; bulk of thickness)
> **F** — **Finish coat** (final surface; thin 3–5 mm)

**Memory hook:** "Scratch the mud, Brown it flat, Finish it smooth." The order never changes — applying a finish coat before the brown coat has cured produces a delaminating, cracked surface. Remember also: brown coat must be **damp-cured** for Portland cement plaster.

---

## 8. Active Recall Questions

**Question 1**
*(LEA Area 2 — Materials & Methods | Subtopic: Gypsum Wall Board)*

A building's corridor wall separating a Type IV office building's egress corridor from adjacent tenant spaces must be fire-rated per the 2004 Revised IRR. Which gypsum board specification correctly begins to satisfy this requirement?

- A. 9.5 mm (3/8") standard gypsum board on both sides of steel studs at 600 mm o.c.
- B. 12.7 mm (1/2") standard gypsum board on both sides of steel studs at 400 mm o.c.
- C. 15.9 mm (5/8") Type X gypsum board on both sides of steel studs at 400 mm o.c. in a tested 1-hour assembly
- D. 15.9 mm (5/8") moisture-resistant gypsum board on both sides of steel studs at 600 mm o.c.

> **Correct Answer: C**
> A 1-hour fire-resistive corridor wall requires a tested assembly using Type X gypsum board (15.9 mm / 5/8") at the stud spacing and fastener pattern prescribed by the assembly. Standard board (Options A and B) and moisture-resistant board (Option D) do not contribute to tested fire-resistance ratings. Per the 2004 Revised IRR, Rule XII, Section 1215, the installation must conform to fire-resistive rating requirements — which means a complete, tested assembly.

---

**Question 2**
*(LEA Area 2 — Materials & Methods | Subtopic: Plaster Types — PH vs. USA Standard)*

A building in Manila requires an exterior plaster finish on concrete hollow block walls. Which specification is correct, and which standard (Philippine or US) is more restrictive regarding minimum total plaster thickness?

- A. Gypsum plaster, 12 mm; PH and USA are equivalent
- B. Portland cement plaster, 15 mm; Philippine practice (15–20 mm) is less thick than the IBC minimum of 22 mm for 3-coat metal lath systems
- C. Lime plaster, 20 mm; USA is more restrictive
- D. Portland cement plaster, 12 mm; Philippine practice exceeds the IBC minimum

> **Correct Answer: B**
> Exterior plaster must be Portland cement plaster (gypsum plaster is interior-only). Philippine practice specifies 15–20 mm for exterior walls, which satisfies PD 1096 requirements. The IBC (Section 2508.1) requires a minimum 22 mm (7/8") for 3-coat exterior Portland cement plaster over metal lath — making the USA standard more prescriptively restrictive for that specific substrate. Option D is incorrect because PH practice (15–20 mm) is less than 22 mm, not exceeding it.

---

**Question 3**
*(LEA Area 2 — Materials & Methods | Subtopic: Section 1215 Framework)*

Under PD 1096 and the 2004 Revised IRR, which two primary rules work together to determine the required lath, plaster, and wall board specifications for a given building element?

- A. Rule III (Permits and Inspections) and Rule XII (General Building Requirements)
- B. Rule IV (Types of Construction) and Rule VI (Fire-Resistive Standards)
- C. Rule V (Fire Zones) and Rule VIII (Light and Ventilation)
- D. Rule X (Sanitation) and Rule XI (Electrical Systems)

> **Correct Answer: B**
> The 2004 Revised IRR, Rule XII, Section 1215 explicitly ties lath, plaster, and wall board installation to (1) fire-resistive rating requirements (Rule VI) and (2) the type of construction (Rule IV). Rule IV determines what types of materials are permitted and whether fire-resistant construction is required; Rule VI specifies the ratings that must be achieved. This two-rule framework is the core of Section 1215.

---

## 9. Cross-Referencing Section

Section 1215 does not exist in isolation. Understanding it requires integrating several layers of the Philippine building code framework and allied legislation.

### Rule IV — Types of Construction (PD 1096)
The most direct cross-reference. Rule IV classifies buildings into Types I through V based on the combustibility and fire resistance of their structural elements. Each type has corresponding requirements for walls, partitions, floors, and roof structures. Section 1215 draws its technical requirements directly from this classification: a Type I building has no fire-resistive requirement for interior partitions; a Type V building requires incombustible, fire-resistive construction throughout. This determines whether any fire-rated lath or wall board assembly is required at all.

### Rule V — Fire Zones (PD 1096)
Fire zones impose additional restrictions based on location within a municipality. In Fire Zone 1 (densely built, high-risk areas), exterior construction materials must be non-combustible. This affects the choice of lath and plaster for exterior walls, ensuring cement plaster over metal lath rather than any combustible lath system. Rule V requirements apply independently of and in addition to Rule IV type-of-construction requirements.

### Rule VI — Fire-Resistive Standards (PD 1096)
Rule VI is the technical backbone of Section 1215. It establishes the fire-resistance ratings required for building elements (walls, columns, beams, slabs) by type of construction and occupancy group. When a wall requires a 1-hour fire-resistance rating per Rule VI, Section 1215 requires that the lath, plaster, or wall board assembly achieve that rating. Rule VI also cross-references to ASTM test methods (E119) and UL assembly listings.

### Rule XII, Section 1204 — Vertical Openings (Shaft Walls)
Elevator, mechanical, and plumbing shafts must be enclosed in fire-rated construction. Shaft walls are a specialized application of Section 1215 requirements: the wall board (typically gypsum liner panels) and lath must be part of a rated shaft wall assembly. These assemblies are tested independently of standard partition assemblies.

### Rule XII, Section 1207 — Exits and Corridors
Corridor walls in most occupancies must achieve a 1-hour fire-resistive rating. This is one of the most frequently tested applications of Section 1215 in practice. The specification of 15.9 mm Type X gypsum board in a tested 1-hour assembly on corridor walls flows directly from the interaction of Section 1207 (requiring the rating) and Section 1215 (requiring the installation to conform to that rating).

### RA 9514 — Fire Code of the Philippines
The Fire Code governs interior finish materials independently of PD 1096. Section 1215 addresses fire-resistive construction (structural fire protection), while RA 9514 governs interior finish flame-spread ratings (surface burning characteristics). A wall board may achieve a 1-hour structural fire-resistance rating but still fail RA 9514 requirements if its exposed surface has a flame-spread index above the permitted limit for the occupancy and location. Both standards must be satisfied simultaneously.

### BP 344 — Accessibility Law
Barrier-free design requires grab bars at accessible toilet and bathing facilities. Grab bars require solid support — gypsum board alone cannot support the required loads (150–200 kg minimum pull-out load per fixture). BP 344 indirectly affects wall board installation by requiring solid blocking (wood or steel) within the wall cavity at prescribed heights. The architect or designer must coordinate blocking requirements during the design of the wall assembly, not as an afterthought during construction.

### NSCP — National Structural Code of the Philippines
While not a direct cross-reference of Section 1215, the NSCP governs the structural framing that supports lath and wall board. In seismic Zone 4 (Metro Manila) and Zone 5 (high-risk regions), steel stud partitions must be designed to accommodate seismic inter-story drift. A clearance of 25–38 mm at the top track is standard practice, preventing the partition from acting as an unintended structural element during seismic events. This gap must be properly firestopped where the partition is part of a rated assembly.

### ASTM and Referral Standards (as adopted under PD 1096)
The following ASTM standards are part of the referral code library applicable under PD 1096:
- **ASTM C36 / C1396:** Gypsum wallboard specifications
- **ASTM C840:** Installation of interior gypsum board
- **ASTM C926:** Application of Portland cement plaster
- **ASTM E119:** Standard fire-resistance test method (basis for fire-resistance ratings)
- **GA-216 (Gypsum Association):** Fire-Resistance Design Manual — the primary reference for tested gypsum board assemblies

---

## 10. Spaced Repetition Prompt

Return to this module in 3 days. If you can answer the Active Recall questions without peeking, advance to the next topic.

Before closing this article, confirm you can do the following from memory:

1. State the exact text of PD 1096, Section 1215 (basic law) and how the 2004 Revised IRR expands it.
2. Name the two rules that Section 1215 cross-references and explain what each provides.
3. Distinguish Type X from standard gypsum board and explain why the rating belongs to the assembly, not the board.
4. Name the three coats of the standard plaster system in order and give a typical thickness for each.
5. Explain why gypsum plaster cannot be used on the exterior of a Philippine building.
6. Apply the **FLAT-CF** and **SMOKE** mnemonics to a new wall board specification scenario.

---

*Article 31 of the LEA Board Exam Review Series | Rule XII, Section 1215 | PD 1096 & 2004 Revised IRR*
*Philippine context: tropical climate, seismic Zone 4/5, CHB construction dominance, fire zone restrictions under Rule V*

---

# Masters of the Golden Age
*An Immersive LEA Review Module*

---

## Learning Goal

<Tip>Focus on the architect's defining philosophy and key built works. The LEA frequently tests the relationship between an architect's theoretical principles and their physical execution in specific buildings.</Tip>

- Identify the four National Artists for Architecture (Nakpil, Antonio, Locsin, Mañosa) in chronological order with their key buildings and signature styles.
- Explain Locsin's "floating volume" concept and Mañosa's Neo-Vernacular philosophy (Filipino values, climate response, indigenous materials).
- Distinguish the contributions of each National Artist and correctly attribute their major works (CCP Complex vs. Coconut Palace, FEU vs. Quiapo Church).

## The Real-World Scenario (The Hook)

You are walking through the CCP Complex along Manila Bay at dusk. To your left, a massive concrete volume seems to hover above a reflecting pool — Leandro Locsin's Tanghalang Pambansa. To your right, the Coconut Palace gleams with indigenous materials — Francisco Mañosa's tropical reinterpretation of the bahay kubo. These two buildings, standing meters apart, represent the twin poles of post-war Philippine architecture: Brutalist internationalism and neo-vernacular nationalism.

---

## Core Concepts

- **The Golden Age of Philippine Architecture (1950s–1990s):** The post-independence era when Filipino architects moved beyond colonial styles to define a distinctly national architectural identity — first through Modernism and Brutalism, then through Neo-Vernacular design rooted in indigenous traditions.
- **The Four National Artists for Architecture:** **Juan Nakpil** (1973), **Pablo Antonio** (1976), **Leandro Locsin** (1990), and **Francisco Mañosa** (2018) — the only four architects to receive the Philippines' highest cultural distinction.
- **The "Floating Volume":** Leandro Locsin's signature design concept — massive concrete forms that appear to levitate above the ground, inspired by the raised floor of the indigenous bahay kubo.
- **Neo-Vernacular Architecture:** Francisco Mañosa's philosophy of grounding modern Filipino architecture in the DNA of the bahay kubo and bahay na bato — using indigenous materials, tropical climate response, and Filipino cultural values.

---

## The Hard Data (Cheat Sheet)

### The Four National Artists for Architecture

| Architect | Lifespan | National Artist Year | Style / Philosophy | Key Buildings | LEA High-Yield Facts |
|-----------|----------|---------------------|-------------------|---------------|---------------------|
| **Juan Nakpil** | 1899–1986 | **1973** (first architect honored) | **Art Deco**; combined stylized flora and angular forms; modernist pioneer | **Quiapo Church** (added dome & second belfry, 1930), **Rizal Theater**, **Capitol Theater**, **UP Administration & Library Buildings**, **Manila Jockey Club**, **Philippine Village Hotel**, **Rizal Shrine (Calamba)**, **Boy Scouts of the Philippines HQ** | First Filipino National Artist for Architecture; co-founded Philippine College of Design (1941, did not survive WWII); worked alongside Pablo Antonio, Andres Luna de San Pedro, and Fernando Ocampo to launch modern architecture in the Philippines |
| **Pablo Antonio** | 1901–1975 | **1976** (second architect honored) | **Art Deco / Early Modernism**; "clean lines, plain surfaces, and bold rectangular masses"; each building deliberately unique | **FEU Campus buildings** (1938–1950, largest surviving Art Deco ensemble in Manila — UNESCO Honorable Mention 2005), **Ideal Theater**, **Life Theater** (1941), **Scala Theater**, **Lyric Theater**, **Forum Theater** | Pioneer of modern Philippine architecture; radical departure from Neoclassicism; designed multiple Manila theaters; FEU campus is his masterwork |
| **Leandro Locsin** | 1928–1994 | **1990** | **Brutalism / Modernism**; signature "**floating volume**" — massive forms hovering above ground, inspired by the bahay kubo's raised floor | **Tanghalang Pambansa / CCP Main Theater** (1966–1969), **Philippine International Convention Center (PICC)**, **Sofitel Philippine Plaza Manila**, **Church of the Holy Sacrifice (UP Diliman)**, **Istana Nurul Iman (Brunei Sultan's Palace)** | The "floating volume" is his most testable concept; CCP Main Theater has three capiz-shell chandeliers representing Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao; also designed the world's largest residential palace (Istana Nurul Iman, Brunei) |
| **Francisco Mañosa** | 1931–2020 | **2018** | **Neo-Vernacular**; "Filipino values, Philippine climate, indigenous materials"; architecture inspired by the DNA of the bahay kubo and bahay na bato | **Coconut Palace / Tahanang Pilipino** (1980, CCP Complex), **San Miguel Corporation HQ** (Ortigas, 1979), **EDSA Shrine** (1989), **Amanpulo Resort** (Palawan, 1994), **Pearl Farm Resort** (Samal Island, 1994), **Mactan Shangri-La Resort** (Cebu, 1993) | Known as the "**Father of Philippine Neo-Vernacular Architecture**"; championed indigenous materials (bamboo, rattan, coconut, anahaw, capiz, volcanic rock); design features: high ceilings, large windows, low eaves, free interior-exterior interchange |

### Design Philosophy Comparison

| Dimension | Nakpil & Antonio | Locsin | Mañosa |
|-----------|-----------------|--------|--------|
| **Era focus** | Pre-war to post-war transition | Post-independence Modernism | Late 20th century identity quest |
| **Primary style** | Art Deco → Early Modernism | Brutalism / International Modernism | Neo-Vernacular / Tropical |
| **Relationship to tradition** | Decorative integration of Filipino motifs into Western frameworks | Abstract reinterpretation of the bahay kubo's spatial concept (floating volume) | Direct physical use of indigenous materials and building forms |
| **Signature material** | Reinforced concrete with Art Deco ornamentation | Raw, exposed concrete (béton brut) | Bamboo, coconut wood, rattan, capiz shell, volcanic rock |
| **scale** | Commercial, institutional, theaters | Monumental civic / cultural | Resorts, residences, ecclesiastical, institutional |

### National Artist Timeline (Chronological Order)

| Year | Recipient | Field |
|------|-----------|-------|
| **1973** | **Juan Nakpil** | Architecture |
| **1976** | **Pablo Antonio** | Architecture |
| **1990** | **Leandro Locsin** | Architecture |
| **2006** | (No architecture awardee) | — |
| **2018** | **Francisco Mañosa** | Architecture |

---

<ExamTip>**LEA Pattern:** Questions about this architect often present an unfamiliar building and ask you to identify the architect based on characteristic details — look for signature elements like cruciform columns (Mies), pilotis (Corbusier), or structural expressionism (Gaudi).</ExamTip>

## LEA Exam Traps and Common Mistakes

- **Trap: Confusing Nakpil and Antonio projects.** Both were Art Deco contemporaries active in the same era. Remember: **Antonio = FEU Campus and theaters**; **Nakpil = Quiapo Church, Rizal Theater, UP buildings**. The exam may pair a Nakpil building with Antonio's name as a distractor.
- **Trap: Attributing the Coconut Palace to Locsin.** Both Locsin and Mañosa have buildings in the CCP Complex. The **Tanghalang Pambansa (CCP Main Theater) and PICC = Locsin**. The **Coconut Palace (Tahanang Pilipino) = Mañosa**. They are different architects with different philosophies working in the same physical complex.
- **Trap: Misunderstanding the "floating volume."** It is NOT about lightweight materials. Locsin used massive concrete — the "floating" effect is an optical illusion created by recessing the base and cantilevering the upper mass. The concept is inspired by the elevated bahay kubo, but executed in Brutalist concrete.

---

## Board-Prep Mnemonics

**"NALO-MA" — The Four National Artists in Chronological Order:**
- **NA** — **Na**kpil (1973)
- **LO** — **Lo**csin (1990)... wait, Antonio comes second:

Better mnemonic — **"N-A-L-M" = Nakpil, Antonio, Locsin, Mañosa** (1973, 1976, 1990, 2018):
> **"Nag-Aaral Lahat ng May-ambisyon"**
> (Tagalog: "All the ambitious ones study") — a fitting reminder for LEA review.

**"FCC" — Mañosa's Three Pillars of Filipino Architecture:**
- **F**ilipino values (family, community, ornamentation)
- **C**limate response (tropical — high ceilings, overhangs, ventilation)
- **C**raft / indigenous materials (bamboo, rattan, coconut, capiz)

---

## Active Recall Questions

**Question 1:**
Which architect's signature concept is the "floating volume" — massive concrete forms that appear to hover above the ground?

A) Francisco Mañosa
B) Juan Nakpil
C) Leandro Locsin
D) Pablo Antonio

> **Answer: C) Leandro Locsin.** The "floating volume" is Locsin's signature — seen most dramatically in the Tanghalang Pambansa (CCP Main Theater), where the concrete mass appears to levitate above a reflecting pool. The concept was inspired by the elevated floor of the traditional bahay kubo.

**Question 2:**
The FEU Campus in Manila is recognized as the largest surviving ensemble of which architectural style, earning a UNESCO Honorable Mention in 2005?

A) Brutalism
B) Neoclassical
C) Art Deco
D) Neo-Vernacular

> **Answer: C) Art Deco.** Pablo Antonio designed the FEU Campus buildings between 1938 and 1950 in the Art Deco style. The campus received a UNESCO Asia-Pacific Heritage Awards Honorable Mention for cultural heritage conservation in 2005.

**Question 3:**
Francisco Mañosa is known as the "Father of Philippine Neo-Vernacular Architecture." Which of the following is his masterwork?

A) Philippine International Convention Center
B) Tanghalang Pambansa (CCP Main Theater)
C) Coconut Palace (Tahanang Pilipino)
D) Manila Metropolitan Theater

> **Answer: C) Coconut Palace (Tahanang Pilipino).** Built in 1980 in the CCP Complex, the Coconut Palace extensively uses coconut wood and other indigenous materials. It embodies Mañosa's philosophy that Filipino architecture must be "true to itself, its land, and its people."

---

*Return to this module in 3 days. If you can answer the Active Recall questions cold, move to the next module.*

---

## Cross‑References

**Le Corbusier Five Points**, **The Bauhaus And International Style**, **Mies Van Der Rohe**, **Pre Columbian Mesoamerica**

# Excavation Foundation and Veneer
## Learning Goal
After reading this article, you should be able to:

Apply PD 1096 and NSCP requirements for excavation shoring, foundation design, and masonry veneer anchorage; calculate minimum footing size by soil bearing capacity and building load; identify when underpinning of adjacent structures is required; and determine anchor spacing and type for adhered and anchored veneer systems.
---

## Module Header

| Field | Details |
|---|---|
| **Module Focus** | Excavation Safety, Adjoining Property Protection, Foundation Design, Retaining Walls & Veneer Systems |
| **Legal Basis (PH)** | PD 1096, Rule XII, Sections 1202–1203; Civil Code Arts. 684–686 |
| **IBC Counterpart** | IBC Chapter 18 (Soils and Foundations), Chapter 14 (Exterior Walls/Veneer) |
| **LEA Area** | Area 2 — Structural Design, Utilities & Materials (30% of exam weight) |
| **Difficulty** | Intermediate |
| **Spaced Repetition** | Review this article on Day 1, Day 3, Day 7, and Day 14 for maximum retention |

---

## Hook Scenario

You are the architect-of-record for a 12-storey mixed-use tower in Makati's central business district. The project site is a tight urban lot with party walls shared on two sides. Your structural engineer orders a 4.50-meter deep excavation for the mat foundation. The property to the north is a heritage-listed 3-storey concrete building from the 1950s — its shallow footings were never designed for adjacent deep excavation.

Before a single backhoe touches the ground, PD 1096 Rule XII, Sec. 1202 activates your legal and professional obligations: written notice to the adjoining owner must be delivered at least 10 days before excavation begins, your team must survey and photograph every visible crack in the adjacent structure, and you are personally responsible for ensuring the neighboring building does not destabilize. When your client asks why the schedule has a 10-day buffer before earthworks, you point to the Code. This article covers everything you must know to pass the board exam — and to protect your neighbors when the shovel hits the ground.

---

## Core Concepts

### Concept 1: The Hierarchy of Excavation Responsibility (Sec. 1202.2.b)

Philippine law makes the party **causing the excavation** solely responsible for protecting adjoining property. If your excavation extends below grade and threatens the stability of a neighboring structure's soil or foundation, you — not the neighbor — must either underpin the neighboring footing or extend your own foundation system to make up for the lost lateral and subjacent support. This responsibility is rooted in **Civil Code Articles 684–686**, which codify the right of every landowner to lateral and subjacent support from adjacent land.

- **Civil Code Art. 684**: No proprietor shall make excavations that deprive any adjacent land or building of sufficient lateral or subjacent support.
- **Civil Code Art. 685**: If excavation is necessary, the excavating owner shall give timely notice to adjacent owners.
- **Civil Code Art. 686**: Support obligation transfers if the adjacent owner refuses access to inspect and underpin their own building — the duty then shifts to the refusing party.

### Concept 2: The 10-Day Notice Rule and Consent Shift (Sec. 1202.2.d–e)

Before any excavation begins, the excavating owner must:
1. Notify all **adjoining property owners in writing** at least **10 days** in advance.
2. Provide access to inspect the adjacent structure and install monitoring devices (telltleas, crack gauges, photographic documentation).
3. Survey and photograph all pre-existing cracks in the adjoining premises (Sec. 1202.2.g).

If the adjoining owner **refuses access** after receiving the 10-day notice, the legal burden for any resulting damage **shifts to the refusing party** (Sec. 1202.2.e). This is a classic board exam trap: the default duty rests with the excavating party, but refusal of access by the neighbor transfers liability.

### Concept 3: Slope and Trench Safety Standards (Sec. 1202.2.h–n)

For permanent excavations and fills:
- **Maximum slope**: 2H:1V (2 horizontal to 1 vertical). Any steeper slope requires a geotechnical engineer's report.
- **Trench exits**: For every trench **≥ 1.50 m deep**, a means of exit must be provided at least every **7.50 m** along the trench length (Sec. 1202.2.n).
- **Public property restoration**: Excavations on public property (streets, sidewalks) must be restored within **48 hours** (Sec. 1202.2.c).
- **Linings**: All excavation walls must be lined with shotcrete, boards, runners, or sheet piles as conditions require (Sec. 1202.2.l), inserted progressively as excavation proceeds and kept tight by wedging or jacking (Sec. 1202.2.m).
- **Drainage**: An intercepting drain is required at the junction of permeable and impervious strata; weepholes at the lowest one-third of the excavation wall provide pressure relief (Sec. 1202.2.i).

### Concept 4: Retaining Wall Requirements (Sec. 1202.3)

Retaining walls are **mandatory** wherever there is an abrupt change in ground levels that could cause soil instability. Per Sec. 1202.3.a, all footings and foundations must be of appropriate type, adequate size, and sufficient capacity to safely sustain all superimposed loads — including **seismic and lateral forces** per the NSCP. The NSCP (National Structural Code of the Philippines) governs seismic design of foundations in Seismic Zone 4 (most of the Philippine archipelago), requiring special detailing for pile caps, grade beams, and retaining wall footings in high-seismicity areas.

### Concept 5: Veneer Design — The 2× Force Rule (Sec. 1203)

Veneer is defined as a **non-structural facing** of brick, concrete, tile, metal, plastic, or glass attached to a backing for ornamentation, protection, or enclosure (Sec. 1203.1). The critical distinction between adhered and anchored veneer:

- **Adhered veneer**: Bond must be sufficient to resist shearing stresses, including seismic forces (Sec. 1203.2.d). No specific force multiplier, but seismic detailing is required.
- **Anchored veneer**: Must be designed to resist **horizontal forces equal to 2× the weight of the veneer** (Sec. 1203.2.e). This 2× factor accounts for wind, seismic, and impact forces acting on the cladding.
- **Anchor materials**: All anchors, supports, and ties must be **non-combustible and corrosion-resistant** (Sec. 1203.2.f) — no galvanized wire in marine environments, for instance.
- **Movement accommodation**: Design must account for differential movements from temperature, shrinkage, creep, and deflection (Sec. 1203.2.c) — especially critical for high-rise towers subject to inter-storey drift.

---

## PH vs. USA Comparative Analysis

The Philippine code (PD 1096) and the IBC approach excavation and veneer from similar philosophical bases but differ in specificity, reference standards, and the mechanisms used to enforce neighbor protection.

| Topic | PH — PD 1096 (Rule XII) | USA — IBC (Chapter 18 / 14) |
|---|---|---|
| **Governing authority** | Building Official under DPWH; Civil Code Arts. 684–686 | Local AHJ; OSHA 29 CFR 1926.652 for trench safety |
| **Neighbor notification** | Written notice ≥ 10 days before excavation (Sec. 1202.2.d) | No explicit advance notice period in IBC; OSHA governs jobsite safety |
| **Geotechnical requirement** | Required when slope exceeds 2H:1V (Sec. 1202.2.h) | IBC Sec. 1803: Geotechnical investigation required per soil classification (ASTM D2487) |
| **Maximum cut slope** | 2H:1V for permanent excavations (Sec. 1202.2.h) | Varies by soil type under OSHA; not specified in IBC body |
| **Trench exit spacing** | Every 7.50 m for trenches ≥ 1.50 m deep (Sec. 1202.2.n) | OSHA: ladder within 7.6 m (25 ft) of workers in trenches ≥ 1.22 m (4 ft) deep |
| **Public ROW restoration** | Within 48 hours (Sec. 1202.2.c) | Varies by local ordinance; not addressed in IBC |
| **Underpinning responsibility** | Excavating party bears full responsibility (Sec. 1202.2.b) | IBC Sec. 1804.1: Excavation shall not reduce support without underpinning |
| **Liability shift** | Shifts to refusing neighbor after 10-day notice and denial of access (Sec. 1202.2.e) | No equivalent IBC provision; governed by tort law |
| **Veneer design force** | Anchored veneer: 2× veneer weight horizontal (Sec. 1203.2.e) | IBC Chapter 14: Anchored masonry veneer designed per TMS 402/602; seismic design per ASCE 7 |
| **Veneer materials** | Non-combustible, corrosion-resistant anchors (Sec. 1203.2.f) | IBC Sec. 1404.2: Corrosion resistance required; stainless steel or hot-dip galvanized |
| **Fills near buildings** | Not placed unless building can withstand loads (Sec. 1202.2.r) | IBC Sec. 1804.2: Backfill free of organic material; compacted per Sec. 1804.3 |
| **Seismic foundation design** | NSCP Chapter 3, Zone 4 (high seismicity) | ASCE 7 Chapter 11–12; IBC Section 1803.5.12 for liquefaction assessment |

**Key Philosophical Difference**: The Philippine code embeds the neighbor-protection obligation directly in the building regulation and ties it explicitly to the Civil Code — making the architect and building owner jointly accountable under both administrative and civil law. The IBC primarily regulates the work itself (soil compaction, geotechnical reports) and defers neighbor disputes to tort law and OSHA jobsite regulations.

---

## Hard Data / Cheat Sheet Table

| Parameter | Value | Code Reference |
|---|---|---|
| Advance written notice to neighbors | ≥ 10 days before excavation | Sec. 1202.2.d |
| Public property restoration time | Within 48 hours | Sec. 1202.2.c |
| Maximum permanent cut/fill slope | 2H:1V | Sec. 1202.2.h |
| Trench depth requiring exit provision | ≥ 1.50 m deep | Sec. 1202.2.n |
| Trench exit spacing | Every 7.50 m along trench | Sec. 1202.2.n |
| Drainage: weepholes location | Lowest 1/3 of excavation wall | Sec. 1202.2.i |
| Slope deviation requirement | Geotechnical report required | Sec. 1202.2.h |
| Retaining walls required when | Abrupt ground level change threatens stability | Sec. 1202.3.b |
| Veneer definition | Non-structural facing; no load except own weight + veneer above | Sec. 1203.1, 1203.2.a |
| Anchored veneer horizontal design force | 2× weight of veneer | Sec. 1203.2.e |
| Adhered veneer bond requirement | Sufficient for shear stress including seismic | Sec. 1203.2.d |
| Veneer anchor material | Non-combustible and corrosion-resistant | Sec. 1203.2.f |
| Civil Code: lateral support right | Every landowner entitled to lateral/subjacent support | Civil Code Arts. 684–686 |
| Liability shift trigger | Adjacent owner refuses access after 10-day notice | Sec. 1202.2.e |
| Alternate section excavation method | Required for long trench excavations | Sec. 1202.2.q |
| Fills near existing buildings | Only if building structure can withstand fill loads | Sec. 1202.2.r |

---

## Cross-Referencing

### NSCP (National Structural Code of the Philippines) — Foundation Design
NSCP Chapter 3 (Soil and Foundations) supplements Sec. 1202–1203 with structural engineering requirements. For seismic design in the Philippine archipelago (predominantly Zone 4), NSCP requires:
- **Soil investigation reports** for all buildings over a threshold height or on soft ground.
- **Special foundation detailing** (pile caps, grade beams, tie beams) for structures in high-seismic zones.
- **Liquefaction assessment** for sites near bodies of water or with loose sandy soils.

The NSCP requirements are the engineering backbone that fleshes out the performance intent of Sec. 1202.3.a ("appropriate type, adequate size/capacity to safely sustain loads under seismic forces").

### Rule VIII (Site, Easements & Site Planning) — Sec. 802–808
Rule VIII governs the physical relationship of a building to its lot and neighboring properties. The setback requirements under Rule VIII determine how close a building can be placed to property lines, which directly influences how deep and how close excavations can be. A building pushed to its minimum setback line will inherently have excavations that extend very close to — or potentially below — the property of the neighbor.

### RA 9514 (Fire Code of the Philippines) — Foundation Compliance
While not directly regulating excavation, RA 9514 and its 2019 IRR govern fire protection systems that require foundation penetrations (standpipe pits, fire pump rooms, underground water storage). These penetrations must be waterproofed and structurally accounted for in the foundation design.

### Civil Code Arts. 684–686 — Legal Foundation for Sec. 1202
The Civil Code provisions are the legal authority that makes Sec. 1202's neighbor protection requirements enforceable beyond mere administrative sanction. A violation of Sec. 1202.2 is also a civil wrong under Art. 684 — meaning the aggrieved neighbor can sue for damages in regular courts, independent of any Building Official action.

---

## Active Learning Techniques

### Memory Aid — "10-2-48-7.5" (The Excavation Sequence)
Anchor all the critical excavation numbers using the sequence **10 – 2 – 48 – 7.5**:

- **10** days: written notice to neighbors before you start
- **2H:1V**: maximum permanent slope ratio
- **48** hours: time to restore public ROW after excavation
- **7.5 m**: maximum spacing between trench exits (trenches ≥ 1.50 m deep)

Say it aloud: *"Ten days, two to one, forty-eight hours, seven-point-five meters."*

### Memory Aid — "2× for Anchored" (Veneer Force Rule)
Anchored veneer must resist horizontal forces = **2× its own weight**. Remember: **ANCHORED = AMPLIFIED**. Adhered veneer relies on bond shear strength; anchored veneer must fight gravity's double.

### If/Then Scenarios

**If** an adjoining property owner refuses to allow your crew to inspect and underpin their building after you gave them written 10-day notice…
**Then** the legal burden of responsibility shifts to that refusing owner per Sec. 1202.2.e — you have documented your compliance with the notice requirement.

**If** the geotechnical report recommends a slope steeper than 2H:1V for a permanently retained cut…
**Then** the deviation is only allowed based on the findings of a geotechnical investigation report per Sec. 1202.2.h — no deviation without documentary support.

**If** an excavation trench is 2.10 m deep and 22.50 m long…
**Then** at least **3 means of exit** must be provided (at 0m, 7.50m, and 15.00m along the trench), with the last exit no more than 7.50 m from any worker's position per Sec. 1202.2.n.

**If** a veneer system uses metal tie anchors in a coastal building…
**Then** all anchors must be non-combustible and **corrosion-resistant** (stainless steel or equivalent) per Sec. 1203.2.f — galvanized anchors alone may be insufficient in high-chloride environments.

---

## Exam Traps

### Trap 1: "Who is Responsible for Underpinning?"
The exam may present a scenario where a neighbor's building is damaged by an adjacent excavation and ask who bears responsibility for extending the neighbor's foundation. The answer is always the **excavating party** — unless the neighbor was given the 10-day written notice and **refused access** to allow inspection and underpinning. If the neighbor refused access, responsibility shifts to them. Watch for whether the notice was given and whether access was denied.

### Trap 2: The 2H:1V Slope Is the Maximum, Not the Standard
The exam may ask for the "required slope" for excavations, tempting candidates to state 2H:1V as a prescribed design value. In fact, 2H:1V is the **maximum allowable** slope — the design must be at least this gentle. Steeper slopes (like 1H:1V or vertical) are prohibited for permanent excavations unless a geotechnical engineer certifies otherwise. Do not confuse "maximum slope" with "minimum slope" — 2H:1V means for every 2 meters horizontal, the cut rises only 1 meter vertical (a relatively gentle grade).

### Trap 3: Veneer Carries No Structural Load (Except Its Own Weight + Veneer Above)
A common distractor involves asking what loads a veneer system must be designed to carry. Veneer by definition is **non-structural**: it carries only its own dead weight and the vertical dead load of veneer panels above it. The backing structure must resist all other loads (wind, seismic, floor loads). For **anchored veneer specifically**, the anchors must resist a **horizontal force = 2× the veneer weight** — this is a lateral load requirement for the connection, not a vertical structural load on the veneer panel itself. Candidates confuse this 2× rule with the veneer carrying structural floor loads, which it never does.

---

## Active Recall Questions

**Question 1**

A high-rise project in Quezon City is set to begin deep excavation immediately adjacent to a 4-storey reinforced concrete residential building owned by a neighboring family. Before any excavation equipment is mobilized, what is the minimum advance notice period the excavating party must provide to the adjoining property owner, and in what form?

A. 7 days, verbal notice to any occupant of the building  
B. 15 days, written notice delivered to the Building Official  
C. 10 days, written notice delivered to the adjoining property owner  
D. 5 days, written notice posted on the project fence  

> **Answer: C — 10 days, written notice to the adjoining property owner**
>
<LawCallout code="nbcp" title="not the Building Official, not a general posting. This 10-day window allows the">

Per PD 1096, Rule XII, Sec. 1202.2.d, the party responsible for the excavation must notify all adjoining property owners in writing at least 10 days before excavation commences. The notice is directed to the property owner — not the Building Official, not a general posting. This 10-day window allows the neighbor to engage their own structural engineer, document pre-existing conditions, and arrange for access. Option A is wrong on both the period (7 days) and the form (verbal). Option B has the wrong period (15 days) and wrong recipient (Building Official). Option D is wrong on the period (5 days) and the method (fence posting is insufficient).

</LawCallout>

---

**Question 2**

During the excavation of a 2.00-meter deep utility trench running 30.00 meters through a project site, the safety inspector asks the site architect how many means of exit (ladders or equivalent) must be provided along the trench per PD 1096. What is the correct answer?

A. 2 means of exit — one at each end of the trench  
B. 3 means of exit — at 0 m, 10 m, and 20 m  
C. 4 means of exit — at 0 m, 7.5 m, 15 m, and 22.5 m  
D. 5 means of exit — at 0 m, 7.5 m, 15 m, 22.5 m, and 30 m  

> **Answer: C — 4 means of exit at 0 m, 7.5 m, 15 m, and 22.5 m**
>
> Per Sec. 1202.2.n, any trench **≥ 1.50 m deep** must have a means of exit at least every **7.50 m**. At 30 m total length, no worker should be more than 7.50 m from an exit, requiring exit points at: 0 m (start), 7.5 m, 15 m, and 22.5 m — that is **4 exits**. A 5th exit at the 30 m end would put it exactly 7.50 m from the 22.5 m exit (just barely acceptable), but the question requires exits every 7.50 m starting from any worker's position, meaning 4 evenly spaced exits cover the trench. Option D over-counts by requiring a redundant end exit. Option B uses 10 m spacing, which exceeds the 7.50 m maximum. Option A provides only two exits — plainly insufficient.

---

**Question 3**

An architect specifies a ceramic tile anchored veneer system on the exterior facade of an 8-storey office building in Metro Manila. The total weight of the anchored veneer on one facade panel is 500 kg. Per PD 1096, Rule XII, Sec. 1203, what minimum horizontal force must the anchor system for that panel be designed to resist?

A. 250 kg (1/2 × panel weight, as veneer is non-structural)  
B. 500 kg (equal to panel weight — dead load equivleance)  
C. 750 kg (1.5× panel weight for seismic factor)  
D. 1,000 kg (2× panel weight per the anchored veneer lateral force requirement)  

> **Answer: D — 1,000 kg (2× the weight of the veneer)**
>
> Per Sec. 1203.2.e, **anchored veneer** must be designed to resist **horizontal forces equal to 2× the weight of the veneer**. For a 500 kg panel, the required horizontal design force is 500 × 2 = **1,000 kg**. This 2× factor accounts for combined wind pressure, seismic forces, and impact loads on the cladding connection. Option A incorrectly halves the weight. Option B applies only a 1:1 ratio (insufficient). Option C uses an arbitrary 1.5× factor that does not appear in the Code. The 2× rule applies specifically to **anchored** veneer — adhered veneer is governed by bond shear strength requirements under Sec. 1203.2.d, not this 2× multiplier.

---

## Spaced Repetition Reminder

**Session 1 (Today):** Read through all core concepts and the cheat sheet table. Write the "10-2-48-7.5" sequence from memory.

**Session 2 (Day 3):** Cover the cheat sheet and recall each value. Work through all three MCQs without looking at the answers first.

**Session 3 (Day 7):** Reconstruct the PH vs. USA comparison table from memory. Focus on the liability shift rule (Sec. 1202.2.e) and the 2× veneer force rule (Sec. 1203.2.e).

**Session 4 (Day 14):** Final review — read exam traps only. If you can explain each trap in your own words without reference to the article, this module is mastered.

*These articles are LEA board exam review materials based on PD 1096 (National Building Code of the Philippines) and cross-referenced with IBC provisions for comparative analysis. Always verify against the current edition of the implementing rules and regulations.*

---

---

## Exam Tip

LEA Swipe: Minimum footing depth = 600 mm below grade (in non-expansive soils). Shoring required when excavation exceeds 2.0 m from property line. Underpinning required when excavation goes below adjacent foundation bottom. Veneer anchors at maximum 400 mm o.c. vertically, 600 mm o.c. horizontally.



---

## Exam Tip

Underpinning required when excavation goes below adjacent foundation bottom. Veneer anchors at maximum 400 mm o.c. vertically, 600 mm o.c. horizontally.



<ArticleMedia id="media-excavation-foundation-and-vene-0" type="image" caption="Excavation and Foundation Protection — Cross-Section with Shoring and Underpinning" description="Cross-section of urban excavation showing: excavation depth with shoring system (sheet piles, soldier piles with lagging), adjoining building footing underpinning (pit method or micropiles), 10-day notice requirement zone, soil bearing capacity testing locations (NSCP Table 304.1), masonry veneer anchorage (tie spacing complying with PD 1096 Rule XVI), and drainage system at foundation base." />

# Widths & Slopes

## Learning Goal

After reading this article, you should be able to:

Calculate minimum required widths for corridors, aisles, exit passageways, and ramps based on occupant load, occupancy group, and accessibility requirements; apply maximum slope ratios for ramps (1:12, 1:15, 1:20) and sidewalk grades; and determine when a ramp is required versus when stairs alone are acceptable.

## 1. Accessible Ramps (BP 344 – Appendix A)

**Width**

- Minimum clear width of **accessible ramps**: **1200 mm**.[file:2]

**Slopes (New Work)** – Table A.1.1: Accessible Ramps

| Slope    | Approx. % | Max Run Length           | Max Rise per Run | Landing Interval                   |
| :------- | :-------- | :----------------------- | :--------------- | :--------------------------------- |
| **1:20** | 5.0%      | – (no rise limit stated) | –                | Landings every **15.0 m**.[file:2] |
| **1:15** | 6.67%     | **10.50 m**              | **700 mm**       | Landings every **10.0 m**.[file:2] |

- Formula: \(\text{Run} = \text{Rise} \times \text{Slope Ratio}\).  
  Example: \(700 \times 15 = 10{,}500\) mm = **10.50 m**.[file:2]

**Landings**

- Intermediate landing required if total ramp length > **10.50 m**.[file:2]
- Minimum length of **intermediate landings**: **1800 mm**.[file:2]
- Level area at **upper and lower ends** of ramp: ≥ **1800 mm** in direction of travel.[file:2]

**Edge Protection & Handrails**

- Raised edge on both sides: **100 mm** min height.[file:2]
- Handrails on **both sides** of ramps at **700 mm and 900 mm** above ramp surface; 300 mm horizontal extension at upper and lower ends.[file:2]

---

## 2. Sidewalks / Walkways / Pathways (BP 344 – Appendix B)

**Widths**

- Minimum width of sidewalks/walkways/pathways: **1500 mm**.[file:2]
- Where space is required for **two wheelchairs to pass**: width = **1800 mm**.[file:2]

**Gradients**

- Along length: “kept as level as possible”; wherever possible, **not steeper than 1:20 (5%)**.[file:2]
- Cross gradient: maximum **1:100 (1%)**.[file:2]

**Turn / Rest / Passing Spaces**

- On lengthy or busy routes, provide spaces with **minimum clear dimension 1800 mm**, at **maximum 12000 mm** intervals.[file:2]
- Turnabout spaces at or within **3500 mm of every dead‑end corridor** (per Appendix B text: “Turnabout spaces shall also be provided at or within 3500 mm of every dead-end corridor”).[file:2]

---

## 3. Curb Ramps & Dropped Sidewalks (BP 344 – Appendix B)

**Curb Ramps**

- Minimum width (drop‑off for PWD at loading bays): **900 mm**.[file:2]
- Maximum gradient: **1:15**.[file:2]

**Dropped Sidewalks**

- Base/level surface at bottom: **1500 mm depth** for crossings/walkways <1500 mm wide; width same as crossing.[file:2]

---

## 4. PD 1096: Ramps as Exits (Context Only)

- “A ramp conforming to the provisions of the Code may be used as an exit. **The width of ramps shall be as required for corridors**.”[file:1]
- Use this together with BP 344: where a ramp is part of an **accessible route**, adopt **≥1200 mm clear** for accessibility even if the PD 1096 corridor minimum is smaller.[file:1][file:2]

---

## 5. Quick Memory Grid

```text
RAMP WIDTH (accessible)     → 1200 mm
RAMP LANDINGS (top/bottom)  → 1800 mm
RAMP INTERMEDIATE LANDING   → 1800 mm (if total > 10.50 m)
RAMP SLOPE (preferred)      → 1:20
RAMP SLOPE (max new)        → 1:15 (10.50 m run, 700 mm rise)

SIDEWALK/WALKWAY WIDTH      → 1500 mm min
TWO-WHEELCHAIR WIDTH        → 1800 mm
REST / TURN SPACE           → 1800 mm; every 12,000 mm
CROSS GRADIENT (sidewalk)   → 1:100
LENGTHWISE GRADIENT         → as level as possible; ideally ≤1:20

CURB RAMP WIDTH             → 900 mm (drop-off)
CURB RAMP SLOPE             → 1:15 max
EDGE PROTECTION (ramp)      → 100 mm
HANDRAILS (ramp)            → 700 & 900 mm high, both sides
```

Use this page to answer any LEA item asking for **minimum widths** or **slopes/lengths** of ramps and primary pedestrian routes based solely on your attached PD 1096 + BP 344 2024 IRR texts.[file:1][file:2]

---

<LawCallout code="bp344" section="Section 7 - Widths and Slopes">


Per BP 344 2024 IRR Appendix A, Table A.1.1: Accessible Ramp Width = 1200 mm minimum clear width. Slope 1:20 (5.0%) — no stated rise limit, landings every 15.0 m. Slope 1:15 (6.67%) — max run 10,500 mm, max rise 700 mm, landings every 10.0 m. Intermediate landings: minimum 1800 mm length. Upper and lower landings: ≥1800 mm in direction of travel.


</LawCallout>

<Warn >

1:12 is the MAXIMUM allowable slope, NOT the standard. The exam will present a question stating 'a ramp with 1:12 slope' and ask if it's compliant. The answer depends on context: 1:12 is acceptable ONLY where space constraints prevent 1:15 or 1:20. If the question doesn't mention space constraints, 1:12 may still be technically compliant as a maximum, but 1:20 is the preferred/ideal.

</Warn>

<ExamTip >

Handrails are required when the ramp rise exceeds 150 mm (about 6 inches). Edge protection (curbs, rails, or extended surfaces) is required on both sides of any ramp with a rise exceeding 150 mm. These are frequently tested together — a ramp exam question often bundles slope, run, landing, handrail, and edge protection requirements.

</ExamTip>

---

## Cross‑References

**Stairs Handrails Guardrails**, **Conflict Matrix Stairs Guards Elevators**, **Bp 344 Ramp Slope Tiers**, **Site Exterior Circulation**
